The House resumed, from March 19, the adjourned debate on the motion of Hon. T. A. Low (Minister of Trade and Commerce) to ratify and confirm a contract between His Majesty and Sir William Petersen providing for the establishment of a subsidized steamship line on the Atlantic, and government control of certain ocean rates, and the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Clark.
Mr. FRANK S. CAHILL (Pontiac):	I
have not read the Preston report, and I do not know Mr. Preston, but I wish to say that if he is responsible for the admissions contained in the reply to the Preston report he is entitled to the gratitude of his Canadian fellow countrymen. This reply dontains enough admissions to convince the country at least that there is a combine known as the North Atlantic Steamship Conference. They start by saying:
The North Atlantic Steamship Conference is not in any sense a combine, but the interests of the large number of individual companies operating steamers from north Atlantic ports required some form of joint action in respect to rates.
So that they admit joint action in respect of rates, and if that is not a combine it must be what was formerly called by the present right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) a monopoly. They admit the combine. We also have the admission of the chief spokesman for the authors of this reply in this House that there is a combine. The right hon. leader of the opposition admitted
Ocean Shipping Rates

the combine. He also stated in 1913 that there was a combine or a monopoly. The monopoly existed in 1913 to such an extent that my hon. friend, as was pointed out by the hon. Minister of National Defence (Mr. Macdonald) yesterday, moved the adjournment of the House to debate the subject, and he said that alarming increases had taken place in the two years, which would be the two years after the 1911 election. My hon. friend made a very good speech on that occasion, a much better speech than the one he made yesterday. And I have noticed in reference to my hon. friend that his best efforts are not put forth when he is declaiming against the interests of the Canadian people. His speech in 1913 was so good a speech that it attracted the attention of the leader of the government of the day, and my hon. friend a few weeks later was taken into that government and proceeded to forget all about the North Atlantic conference. He then started climbing the ladder of fame and kicking out the rungs as he went up. He went on climbing from that time, and forgetting the interests of the Canadian people unil he reached the pinnacle of his political ambition and became the leader of a great party; and when time compelled him to again appeal to the country he found that he had so forgotten the interests of the Canadian people that the electors of tli >
r-r'ntry merely returned a corporal's guard of t-uat once great party to this parliament, minus the corporal. The right hon. gentleman (Mr. Meighen) said at that time:
In my opinion the time has come when not only this House but the country should have that importance impressed upon them.
Speaking of the combine he further said:
The responsibility will rest upon this government; they will be loaded with it only if they should not avail themselves of any remedy within their reach to relieve the present situation.
And he went on further to say:
Whatever may be the difficulties of the solution, its magnitude will demand that it be attempted.
So that even in 1913 the subject of the North Atlantic conference was one which was agitating the minds of the Canadian people. My hon. friends opposite were then in power, and they attempted to do something about it. Another distinguished member of the Conservative party made his first official trip to Europe as a delegate to try to arrange with the British government to control the rates on the north Atlantic. My lion, friend the member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton), then chairman of the railway commission, made a trip, and returned

to say that he could not accomplish anything. He made subsequent trips but accomplished nothing further, save getting for himself a knighthood, and he and the government promptly forgot all about the North Atlantic conference. It was stated then that my hon. friend in reviewing his career did think of his first rung of the ladder and decided he should do something about it, either write a letter to the Times or to Dr. Magill; so he sat down and wrote a letter to Dr. Magill, and then he promptly forgot all about it. He did not even expect a reply to the letter. Certainly he expected no report, and never thought of the letter again until this question was before the House at this session, when he demanded of the government of the day the production of a reply to his Letter to Dr. Magill. That was the sum and substance of his effort towards controlling the North Atlantic combine, but during all that time the Conservative government of the day, for the ten years they were in power, continued to grant subsidies to the ocean shipping combine. They granted subsides of $2,000,000 a year for several years of their tenure of office. They granted in all in the ten years more than $18,000,000 or $1,800,000 a year.. The present subsidy added to the subsidy that is now in the estimates for the current year amounts to only $1,900,000. So I wonder why all the uproar about this particular subsidy! Is it because it is not going to the friends of my hon. friends opposite? Is it because there is to be something in this subsidy for the benefit of the Canadian people? They paid the subsidies I have indicated and nothing was said about the matter. There was no question of rate control. The only "control" that was thought of was control of the money, and that was left to the people who got it. But my hon. friends attack this now as being a waste of the taxpayers' money. They thought nothing of that when they themselves were paying out more money which did not give any advantage to the Canadian people. They attack it because they say it will not be effective. The leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) in 1913 had a remedy. His remedy-he was speaking then, of American rates-was as follows:
I refer to it in order to suggest that perhaps that by the joint operation of both governments, with the co-operation if necessary of the British government, a tribunal might be formed that would be able to control freight rates on the north Atlantic in something the same way in which the railway commission controls railway rates in Canada.
After ten years of doing nothing his friend the hon. member for Burrard (Mr. Clark) produces the same old film and decides to

shoot another picture from it. He moves practically the same motion that they incubated for ten years when they found they were trying to hatch a nest egg. The hon. member for Burrard moves:
That Mr. Speaker do not now leave the chair, bait that it be resolved: That effective control of ocean rates can be exercised only with ,tihe co-operation of all portions of the empire, and by a body on which all are represented.
That is the thing which they have been at for ten years, and in regard to which they could not accomplish anything. Now they propose to form another League of Nations to deal with this matter. Of course, they know it is futile; that nothing can be done along that line; but it would have this result that it would save their friends in the combine from any hardship under this legislation. It would not hurt any person; it would still allow them to go on as they have been doing during the ten years; it would allow them to collect those exorbitant rates which the leader of the opposition said in 1913 were so alarming, and which he said last night had increased 47 per cent since that time. But now he says: It is all right; rates are not too high after all. He argued last night just as the reply of the steamship lines argued. First they admit the combine; second, they admit that rates are high; but they say that they must have high rates in order to make adequate returns. That is all that any person wants, as long as he is allowed to determine what is "adequate."
Then the right hon. member proceeded to argue that rates had not increased very much. That is exactly what the reply does. That is exactly what the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) said. There does not seem to be any argument except-leave it alone, do not interfere with this huge combine. They argue that there is no way of enacting legislation that can control ocean rates. If you cannot enact legislation that will control ocean rates, what other remedy is there? That means that there is only one" remedy-competition. How are you to get competition? My right hon. friend asks: Why not use the mei'chant marine? He suddenly discovered that there was something valuable in the merchant marine. He was exercised over this question for ten years. Why did he not try the merchant marine? He did not do so, but he chooses one of his supporters to move an amendment to create a tribunal of all the governments of the empire and then, in his own speech, he proposes that the merchant marine be put on to break this combine. Why did he not move that as an amendment to this resolution if he thinks so much of the merchant marine? Why did he not move that the total fleet of the merchant marine be put on the north Atlantic? I notice that he does not seem to think veiy much of the merchant marine. He is quite calm about it. But he does, on occasion tell us that the Liberal party were just as strong in support of the merchant marine as he was at the time it was inaugurated. As hon. members will remember, when the merchant marine was inaugurated, the war was on. The merchant marine was inaugurated in 1918, and the first vote on the subject was not opposed by the then Liberal opposition, but it was strenuously opposed in the next session after the war was over; it was more strenuously opposed in the following session; and in the final session my right hon. friend had to put through his vote by closure. That is the kind of "support" which the Liberal party gave to his merchant marine that cost this country 870,000,000 and that my right hon. friend does not seem to think very much of, -yet that he now advocates should be put on the north Atlantic in order to break the combine.
My right hon. friend chided the government for not taking action sooner on the McMaster report. He thought the government was subject to censure for not taking action sooner. I agree with him to some extent. I think a Liberal government that could not accomplish more in ten months than a Tory government could in ten years is somewhat liable to censure. The Liberal government is, I think, making an attempt, but it should be able to accomplish more in a few months than my hon friends opposite could in a whole lifetime.
Hon. gentlemen opposite are attacking Preston; they are attacking the merchant marine; they are attacking the management of the merchant marine; they are attacking everything but the resolution that should be the means of reducing rates on the north Atlantic. If the outcome of this resolution will not be a reduction in the rates, what can be done about the matter? The leader of the opposition yesterday said: We have no right to attempt to control rates on the Atlantic. Where does he get that theory, that a country has no right to control rates on its exports and imports? Such a statement is absurd, and it will be taken as an absurd statement by the people of the country when they have a chance to pass on it. Of course, the people of Canada have a right to control the transportation of their commodities both in and out of this country. There is only one effective way of regulating the rates and that is by competition. If you cannot control your own shipping, if you cannot put on your own boats, and now must adopt other means,

I do not believe the merchant marine could compete; in the first place, they have not the docking facilities in Europe, and, second, they are not fitted for this trade. These boats built by the Petersen company will have the docking facilities and will be built for the trade; they will be an effective factor in reducing rates on the north Atlantic, and the government of the day will be congratulated by the Canadian people for putting through this legislation and will be rewarded for their efforts when the time comes at the next election.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise for the purpose of opposing the resolution now before the House. I do so for various reasons, the principal being that to my mind no necessity has been shown for this legislation, and no proof produced that it would accomplish the purpose for which it has been introduced.
The last speaker (Mr. Cahill) has laid great stress upon the alleged fact that there is at the present time a shipping combination on the Atlantic. There is no question of doubt that there is an Atlantic conference, but it is questionable whether this conference has a malignant influence. We should remember that the various shipping concerns using our ports must have some arrangement whereby shipping may be more or less regular; this is most essential to the trade, and for this purpose at least a conference is necessary. True, the government endeavoured to prove that there was a combine oppressing the shippers of Canada, and for this purpose they had our friend Mr. Preston go over to the Old Country to investigate and report. But the government did not wait for his report. They made a bargain with Sir William Petersen some weeks or months before Mr. Preston submitted his report, trusting that what it contained would justify their action. But we now find that not one single member of the government has treated the Preston report as being reliable. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Low) in introducing the bill quoted from various files of the department showing that investigations had been made in the past, and he relied largely on an 'investigation made by the committee on Agricultural Conditions of a few years ago; but not for one moment did he say that he pinned his faith to the Preston report.
I think, Mr. Speaker, the country is entitled to a thorough investigation before it is committed to an expenditure of many millions of dollars. This experiment will be costly to us. Further, it can have no real value in defeating the combine, if there is one;

on the other hand it may injure our trade very materially. For instance, if there is a combine, the shipping companies forming it might say; We will withdraw our ships from the St. Lawrence for one week. What would the result be? We would have a repetition of the situation on the Great Lakes two years ago, when this government undertook to regulate lake shipping rates, and had ultimately to beg United States vessel owners to come to their rescue and violate the law which had been enacted at the instance of the government itself.
It is significant that if there has been a combine on the Atlantic, the government has actually been a member of that combine, until the last few days at least; so have been the Shipping Board of the United States and the Canadian Pacific Railway Steamship service. And yet we have no evidence that the government made anything out of the operation of the merchant marine even under the combine. Then again, the government has for two years had full opportunity to withdraw their ships; indeed, they had before them a recommendation made by a committee of this House headed by the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster), which brought in a report in these words:
The committee desire to bring the facta in this regard to the earnest attention of the House, and to respectfully suggest that the Minister of Railways and Canals should take the matter up with those responsible for the management of the boats, so that the complicity of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine in this combine may be brought to an end immediately.
Yet in spite of this recommendation the government continued to operate the merchant marine in the combination, and the excuse given by the Prime Minister in the present debate was this:
I am told-I speak subject to correction-that one of the operations of this combine is, that if any line withdraws from it it will immediately attempt to undertake to put that line completely out of business.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the only way in which a combination could put one of its member companies out of business would be by reducing freights to an unprofitable point. The boats of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine also have a greater speed than the majority of the boats mentioned by the Minister of Trade and Commerce,-they have greater horse power and in every way are better equipped. because the vessels happened to be built by the Union government. As a matter of fact, these boats cost too much; there is no question about that. What the ships need is more cargo; that has been their only trouble in the past, and the only reason they are not making money now is that they are not given sufficient cargo to carry. How can we secure that cargo? What chance have our boats against the boats of the combine or of any other line of steamships which have regularly established offices in foreign countries? The very fact that this government kept them in the combine was injurious to the merchant marine, because naturally these agents had affiliations throughout the country and directed trade to the boats with which they had had dealings for many years. The only way our merchant

marine could have succeeded; the only way it can succeed now, would be to give some inducement to the public to patronize the vessels. If the government would give a lower rate, nfaking a ten per cent reduction in freight rates as compared with the other lines, the merchant marine ships would be filled with cargo. Is it not better to have a steamer filled at ninety cents than half-filled at a dollar? The management is the same, the overhead is the same; and the only way to make the marine a success is to see that it is properly represented abroad and to give a freight rate that will induce shippers to patronize it.
Not satisfied with keeping our boats in the combine, if there is a combine, the government went further. I would refer hon. gentlemen to a sentence or two quoted by the Minister of Trade and Commerce in his speech on this subject, which will be found at page 717 of Hansard. The statement he quoted is as follows:
I feel that the steamship companies, including the Canadian merchant marine, are only preventing trade coming to them by demanding such exorbitant freight rates, and I sometimes think that the Canadian merchant marine are the worst sinners of the lot.
The correspondent goes on to give instances in which he had found it cheaper to ship by other lines rather than by our own boats.
I shall say a few words now regarding the contract itself. The country is obligated to pay at the rate of 816,600 per voyage regardless of the number of ships operated. If Petersen puts on one ship he gets a bonus; if he puts on ten ships he gets ten times as much; and it is not necessary for him to make any particular number of voyages per month or in a year. Sir William Petersen may make three or four voyages per year and he gets the same bonus;. so that instead of $16,000 odd per voyage the amount he will get will be double or treble that sum. Let us take it on the other basis. Sir William Petersen invests a certain sum of money; at the end of ten years he has a full return for every cent of principal and interest invested and has $6,000,000 over and above 4 p.m. that. And he has his ships entirely free of debt. There can be no question therefore about the advisability of the contract from Sir William Petersen's point of view; I should imagine that he and his associates would be most anxious to have it go through. So far as the people of the country are concerned, however, I can see no possible reason why they should be compelled to make a gift of that kind to him. There is absolutely no reason for it.

Now a word as to the fixing of rates. We were told, I think by the Minister of Agriculture, that the government would fix all rates; and the Prime Minister informed us that the government would select certain commodities. I do not care which horn of the dilemma they take, whether they decide to reduce the rates on all commodities or to reduce them on certain articles only, what I want to know is: how will the government reduce the rates at all or how will they find out on what commodities they should be reduced? As a matter of fact, it would be utterly impossible to lower rates by a certain percentage pro rata throughout; and we have no means of knowing whether the rates are profitable or unprofitable so far as the shipping companies are concerned. The government themselves do not know whether or not certain of the main articles of export come under the combine at all; they do not know to-day. There is not a man who has stood up in this House who will either affirm or deny that wheat, one of our principal articles, is free from the combination. I myself do not know; it is not my place particularly to know; but it would be my place to find out before making a treaty of this kind.
Before closing I want to re-affirm what I said before, that it is most desirable that the merchant marine should be put into open competition with the combine, if there is one, and that we should give the ships a fair chance to make money, and see whether by that means we cannot accomplish the end which is sought by the present legislation. I would point out again that the merchant marine is charged against the people at the rate of approximately $200 a ton, while the real value to-day is probably one-quarter of that. The people are charged with five per cent depreciation on that inflated value, and they are charged also five and one-half per cent interest not only on the money invested but on all back deficits. So that every time they go in the hole the interest is added on to the succeeding year. Now, it is not possible as a business venture to get along that way. There is not a business man either in this House or in the country who after the war did not write down his assets to an ordinary commercial value; if he did not he went out of .business, he could not carry on. Why should we not do the same in the case of the merchant marine? I have no mud to throw at any scheme; I have no brief for the Canadian merchant marine; but I do think that we should give it a decent chance to live and see whether we cannot accomplish results.

It has been stated that they have been killing trade, and many other statements of that description have been made. These steamship men will have an opportunity of appearing before that committee and of justifying their charges, if they claim they can be justified; and if they are not justified in charging these rates, we will perhaps be able to place before these steamship men and other witnesses appearing before the committee certain means whereby not only the country but the steamship companies can be assisted, and be allowed to go on with their business in a just and reasonable way.
Let me make it quite clear, Mr. Speaker, that my intention in voting for this resolution is to ventilate the situation and be seized of all the possible intricacies of transportation rates, and so be in a position to advise my constituents as to what should be done in the interests of the country as a whole. That is the position which I have already taken in the city of Montreal, and it is the position which I intend to adhere to. I want the information and proof placed before me so that I can substantiate in every just and reasonable way the position which I have already taken. If this resolution to me meant the depriving of any company or

any individual of any right that they were reasonably and properly entitled to exercise in the course of their business, I doubt very much whether I would support it, but I do not think it will have that effect.
Let me for a moment remind hon. gentlemen in the briefest possible terms of what I said in the debate on the Address. At that time after considerable study and, I think, with correctness, I analyzed to t'he best of my ability the financial situation of the Dominion, and the conclusion which I then reached on the figures submitted-which I in no way intend to re-submit to-day-was that until our railways could be made to pay we would have no chance in the world of reducing the taxation which the country needs in the very worst possible way. In order to make our railways pay, I quoted the old and oft repeated phrase, that we had to have more people in this country. But I added that we could not retain our present population, much less could we expect to get newcomers, unless those who were here could profitably live by means of their production.
I stated at that time in the most positive terms that any immigration policy would fail, no matter how wisely conceived and how efficiently carried out, unless the immigrants brought here could profitably produce and live in reasonable comfort. Otherwise they would not stay, and consequently we would not only lose our population but it would be impossible to secure others to take their place, and any money spent on immigration would therefore be wasted. Those opinions I stated again in the city of Montreal on the fifteenth of December last, and I repeat them to-day.
Following down the idea underlying those opinions, Mr. Speaker, can you tell me how we are to have profitable production in certain sections of the Dominion unless we have reasonable transportation rates? How can we, looking at the map of Canada and realizing the way our population is scattered over such a far-flung area-how can we, I say, expect those people to be successful unless they have reasonable transportation rates to get their products to the point where they are to be marketed? I said then that it was not a question to me of Crowsnest pass rates, nor, I may add, of combine rates; to me the question is that these rates, both ocean and rail, must be fixed in such a way as to enable the products of the country to Teach their market so they can compete with like products from other countries. Further, I said-and I have repeated it in my own constituency-that

perhaps the railways and the steamship companies could not give such rates and continue in operation. I believe that these transportation companies should be allowed to live, and I do not think any fair-minded man would deny that they should have sufficient remuneration for the services they have to sell. But if the transportation companies cannot give us the low rates I have in mind, and continue in operation, then some other means will have to be found to bring down transportation rates to a point that will enable our products to reach their market at a profit to their producers.
That brings me, it is true, to the question of subsidies. Hon. gentlemen need not doubt my opinion in this regard. I do not think subsidies are economic in many ways, but we have to take into consideration not what perhaps at the moment is the most economic way. As a matter of fact we have not an economic country to develop. Our natural market for many of our products of the west is a few miles to the south; that is the natural market for much of our Alberta coal and other products of the west. But can we get that market? No. Therefore we have to haul those commodities across the continent in a most uneconomical way and then transport them across the ocean in order to reach their point of market. And therefore when we talk about subsidies, although they may be uneconomic, still they are necessary, I claim, in order to bring transportation rates down to a basis sufficiently low to take our products to the final destination where they can be marketed. It is quite true that it may be possible to do without subsidies to some extent, to so balance up our transportation rates both by land and by water that certain commodities will be made to bear a little heavier rate and allow other basic commodities a necessarily lower rate. That is what I want to find out, and this special committee will enlighten me because transportation experts will appear and tell us whether it is possible or not to make transportation rates on the basis I have suggested.

He first of all asked for leave to move the adjournment of the House for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance, a proceeding which, as hon. gentlemen are very well aware, is, to say the least of it, a very unusual proceeding, a proceeding which predicates at least that there is a very important matter to bring before the government, one which should not be put off for two or three years, but which is to be taken up at once. In moving that adjournment he-
Asked for leave to move the adjournment cf the House, for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance, namely, the rapid and alarming increase in rates on the north Atlantic and the duty of the government in relation thereto.
Now I am not assuming the attitude of any partisan in so far as the matter of steamship companies is concerned. I am not at this moment criticizing their rates and I am not criticizing their means of procedure, and I am not saying that the Petersen contract as submitted to the House in the form it now stands is the most satisfactory manner of solving this problem, but what I say is that if in 1913 this matter was one of great urgency, it is far more urgent now, because the difficulty of the situation in this country has increased more and more in the way of taxation and expenditure, by reason of the fact that we have acquired many miles of railways that we must feed, which means that the question of profitable production and profitable markets is far more important now than it was in 1913. I do not think anybody can deny that assertion. Following on in that speech my hon. friend said:
Whatever may be said upon that score, there can be no question that the subject is one of great and increasing importance.	[DOT]
Further on he says:
With the exception of the United States of America, no country is so vitally interested in ocean rates on the north Atlantic as is the Dominion of Canada. We import very largely from the United Kingdom; we sell a great part of our surplus products to the United Kingdom. On the reasonable level-
I ask hon. gentlemen to mark these words. -on the reasonable level of ocean rates depends to an enormous extent the profits from that trade, and consequently depends to an enormous extent the prosperity of this country.
Let me repeat to my hon. friends opposite that I am not quoting the right hon. leader of the opposition in any contentious or malignant manneT, or with any idea of making party conflict or with any party idea.. I quote these opinions because I respect them.

I believe these opinions at that time were well considered. I believe at the present time we have to consider precisely the same questions which were brought up in this debate in 1913; that we have to understand them and to settle them; that we must not take the attitude in a childish way that there are in this country certain people, owners of steamships who are not doing right; but we must ask those owners of steamships to come before this committee, as they will come, and state their case in fairness and equity to this committee, so that we, as representatives of the people of Canada, can try, if possible, to make rates which will be fair to them and fair to us also. Further on, my right hon. friend who now leads the opposition said, also in clear terms:
Whatever may be the difficulties of the solution, its magnitude will demand that it be attempted.
Then he gives a statement of rates. Further on, in the closing remarks of his address, he stated that at that time he thought a monopoly existed, and stated also in very clear and precise terms that he thought the question of monopoly should be looked into. He stated this not in arrogant or unreasonable terms, but in the same terms as I am speaking in this House to-day, that we need, desire and want information on this subject before we enter into any new contract, and also with the object in view that we shall attempt to make these rates, if possible, what they should be.
Curiously enough, the same attitude was taken in that debate by my friends in the Conservative patty. Hon. George Perley, now Sir George Perley, was Acting Minister of Trade and Commerce in those days. The debate of which I speak was most protracted, but my right hon. friend (Mr. Meighen), who at that time was a simple private member, used these words which are most significant and which I share in every respect:
At all events, the purpose of my bringing this discussion up is to draw the attention of the people of this country through this parliament to the great increase that has taken place, to call attention to the serious aspect of this matter in relation to our prosperity and to enlist behind the government the active co-operation and sympathy of the Canadian people in whatever steps they may see fit to take in order to bring about a betterment of conditions.
That is the stand which I take on the floor of this House to-day. I want to enlist the sympathy of all members of all parties in this House in a non-partisan movement, if it is possible to make such a movement, in order to investigate and to inquire into this situation, to see if it exists, and if it does exist-, to see if we cannot better it. No hon. gentleman can deny the fairness of that

attitude. No one in the city of Montreal, not even my hon. friends who are in the steamship business, can deny the fairness of that attitude. Nobody can meet me in my constituency and say that I want to do anybody any harm, or that I am trying to do something that is not right. All I say is, using again the words of my right hon. friend: Let all the people in Canada clarify their views and come forward and see if this situation cannot be bettered for the general good of the whole country. What does this mean-the general good of the whole country? What is the use of us in the city of Montreal stating that we there shall not have an investigation in order to ascertain whether this is right or wrong? Is the welfare of the city of Montreal not bound up with the welfare of the whole country? Some people do not think so.

I am not one of those who say that any one fixed policy is good for the whole country. What I say is that this whole country has to move forward as one country and we must develop it in the fairest and most reasonable way with a view to all its interests.
But continuing this discussion, as I stated a moment ago, the debate of the 5th May, 1913, took a considerable time. At that time Sir George Perley was Acting Minister of Trade and Commerce, and subsequently he was Canadian High Commissioner. What were his words in 1913? What did he think of the attitude of my right hon. friend who at that time was a private member and who brought this matter before the House? Did he oppose it? Not at all. These were the words Sir George Perley used, and the words were well used in reference to the statement made by my right hon. friend:
I think the thanks of this House are due to the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen) for bringing up this question in such a fair and nonpartisan way.
That is the same way that I speak in this House to-day-in a fair and non-partisan way. That is why I have no hesitation in asking every hon. gentleman in this House to view this great question in a fair and non-partisan way, so that we can discuss it and understand exactly what the situation is. Sir George Perley continues:

I believe this is one of the most important problems that we have to face in Canada to-day, the question of ocean rates on our produce going to the Old Country. Western members have chiefly spoken on the question of ocean rates, and I am rather sorry the discussion was not confined to that particular phase of the transportation problem.
Then he goes on:
The transportation problem is one of the greatest problems, perhaps the greatest, that we have to face in Canada.
Mark these words, my hon. friends. I have quoted them time .and time again. They contain my views, for what my views may be worth, but they are words we should all mark well. Sir George Perley continues:
We have built great canals, we have spent money on our railways and we have taken the step of providing a railway commission to regulate rates, a commission of which I think we are all justly proud.
He goes on to say that the commission is performing its duty efficiently. But what I want to draw to the attention of hon. members is this: We have our railway system, our canal system, our highway system. What good is all the money that has been spent on all these systems going to be unless we have people in Canada to use these systems? How are we going to keep people in this, country and put them on the farms or anywhere else, unless their production is profit-' able? No hon. member, looking at a map of this Dominion, can say that the question of transportation, particularly the bridging and going across of that vast expanse of rock that runs west of Sudbury for some hundreds of miles, with the geographical problems we have before us, can be considered in the same way that the question of transportation is considered in the United States which has a large intermediate market before the products of that country reach the seaboard. We have not that market; we cannot stop at the seaboard; our produce has to go over the ocean before it reaches its market, and that is the question we have to consider now.
In the same debate Sir Robert Borden, who was then Mr. Borden and who if I mistake not, was Prime Minister, also emphasized previously the same point. These were the closing words of his remarks:
A country such as this, which has a great export trade in agricultural products, particularly in cereals, notably in wheat and in flour, is undoubtedly deeply interested in the establishing of reasonable freight rates, and no matter could more worthily engage the attention of parliament than the bringing about of any legislation which might tend to remove any injustice or hardship in this regard that may have been created in the past or that may exist at present.
So I say, I gather a great deal of encouragement from that particular debate.

I myself stated in the
city of Montreal on December 15 that, in order to allow the products of the west and of the Maritime provinces to reach their markets profitably, transportation rates should be so fixed, if necessary, as to have them borne in part by the country as a whole. That

opinion which I expressed at that time has been repeated by others; it has been commented on in this House by the Prime Minister and it has been repeated also in the daily press. I would ask this question: What is the use of levelling transportation rates on land if we leave the rates up in the air at the end of the land? Why not continue the levelling process so that the products may be subject to a reduced rate on board 5 p.m. ship until they finally reach their market? It seems to me that this line of argument is reasonable; and as I suggested it in the city of Montreal, and as others have suggested the same thing elsewhere, I think it would be futile for me or any other gentleman who has taken that view to come before the House and say, "Yes, we should level transportation rates on land to a certain figure and if necessary have the whole country bear the cost; but we must not carry that principle further and also attempt to have our ocean rate structure made in such a way as to be compatible with land rates in order that the same products shipped from the same place, in the prairie section of the country for example, might reach Liverpool, Dundee, Aberdeen or any other port on the same equitable basis." I do not think that such an attitude is rational. In order to establish some parity between land and ocean rates the government has brought down, as a basis for discussion, a certain contract made between it and Sir William Petersen. That contract is at present before parliament in the shape of a resolution and will later be embodied in a bill.
But mark this:	the contract is subject to
ratification by parliament. There is a special clause in the agreement providing that it shall be ratified, and until it is so ratified it does not become a contract at all. The government have not come forward in any unreasonable attitude. They do not say: "Here is a contract, take it or leave it. We do not care what members on this side or opposite may think about it; we do not care what their attitude may be. We have made the contract and it is for you to take it or leave it; but you shall have nothing more whatever to say about it and nothing further to do with it." From the very initiation of this debate the government declared that the contract would be submitted to a special committee for consideration and that that committee would have every means of thoroughly examining into the agreement to decide whether it was good or bad. That statement was repeated by the Prime Minister in his address the other day. Exception has been taken to

Ocean Shipping Rates
that stand on the part of the government as one that is not characteristic of other parliaments; it is said that other contracts having been entered into by a government, and having been signed and sealed, they have simply been submitted to parliament to be accepted or rejected as parliament might see fit. That is not the attitude of the government in the present instance. And what is the difference? In those days when other contracts were ratified the questions involved were entirely different from the one under consideration now. It was not then a matter of building up a general scheme of transportation rates; it was not a matter of production on a large scale; it was not a matter in which the profitable livelihood of the people at large was at stake.	All these things are vitally involved in the present contract and therefore it is only fitting that the government should afford parliament, through a special committee, an opportunity of studying the contract from every point of view and of offering such amendments as may suggest themselves. And I am free to admit that had the contract been brought down in such a way as to preclude discussion, had I been asked to accept a grave situation of this kind without the fullest means of investigation, I should have hesitated before committing myself. But that is not the case, and that has been made perfectly clear, to me at least, in the Prime Minister's statements. The Prime Minister declared, at page 1212 of Hansard:
Whether the method which the government is taking to control ocean rates may be effective or not is a subject which, I think, admits of debate and which should be discussed fully and carefully.
He then points out what the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Low) had said.
The agreement which the government has made with Sir William Petersen with respect to placing on the Atlantic the ten ships mentioned, will be sent to a special committee of this House, together with the bill in which it is included, for full consideration, and that hon. members will have the opportunity afforded by such a select committee to weigh carefully all sides of that agreement, and to pass upon it, only after they have thoroughly considered it.
These words of the Prime Minister are, I think, of considerable weight. But there is more than that. I quote from page 1213:
The point I wish to make clear at the moment is that the government was careful in presenting this resolution to indicate at the outset that the intention was that, once the resolution was carried and the bill introduced and given second reading, it would be referred to a select committee of the House on which there would be representatives of the different parties in parliament, and that such committee would have all the powers which belong to a select committee of parliament, to investigate and consider the merits of the particular proposition submitted.
And further on the Prime Minister says:
I want to make that clear because I have noticed in the course of the debate that some hon. members have felt some hesitancy about supporting the resolution as introduced, fearing that they were committing themselves in some way to the specific terms of the contract.
To revert to what I said at the commencement of my remarks: Here is a contract submitted by this government as a basis for discussion, to be referred to a special committee so that we as a whole can come to a decision whether the contract is a wise and fair bargain for this country to enter into.
There is another point I want to take up, and it is a point which more or less concerns myself and my own constituency. I do not take it up for that purpose, because I say quite frankly I believe that the question of transportation rates should be solved and must be solved. But I want to make this point also clear: Many of my friends are heads of steamship companies. I respect them; I am sure they are honourable men in every way and I believe they are doing the best they can in their own way to develop this country. I for one would not like to see anything done which would deprive them of what is their fair and just due. Does this contract deprive any steamship company or any persons operating steamships of what is their fair and just due? I do not think it does, because provision is made in this contract for the making of a similar arrangement with other companies. Further than that, the Prime Minister in his address on the seventeenth instant, page 1215 of Hansard, says:
And may I say here, Mr. Speaker, that the government has made it known from the outset that it was prepared to make a similar contract with any shipping company in this country that was prepared to give it like terms. The government to-day is prepared to give the Canadian Pacific Steamship Company and other steamship companies doing business out of Canadian ports, the opportunity of entering into a contract along identical lines with the Petersen contract, if they are prepared to do the same as Sir William Petersen is prepared to do.
That is perfectly clear. If any steamship company, learning how the rates are to be made under this Petersen contract, come before this committee and offer to do the same thing, a like contract may be made with them. It may be urged by some of the steamship companies that the government will establish rates which are unfair, but I do not think that is the point in question. Anyone who is accustomed to reading contracts and acts of parliament will know that matters of this description have to be put in more or less general terms, and when the government invites other steamship companies to come forward and agree to a similar

arrangement, that does not mean that the government intends to give them anything other than a fair deal. I think my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) will confirm that.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN-MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to take this opportunity of congratulating the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Low) on his rapid advancement to the important post of First Lord of the Admiralty; and after listening to the splendid speech of my hon. friend from St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Marler), whom I think I may regard as the junior Lord of the Admiralty, I have no doubt that one of the ten ships of the Petersen fleet will be named after him.
The question of ocean rates and their regulation is not a new one. It has been the subject of prolific inquiry and discussion since 1896. Are rates too high? Can they be reduced? And how? Is there a combine? A monopoly? A restraint of trade? In bringing down this contract the government ask us to validate it. But it is already signed, sealed

and delivered by the two parties thereto, His Majesty the King, represented by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Low), and Sir William Petersen, and is enforceable in the Exchequer Court of Canada. Now the government say the contract cannot be varied and that they are prepared to stand or fall by it. This is their plan to bring about a reduction of ocean rates. Well, there are three or four ways of attempting relief- One, by the appointment of a .yaint imperial board, similar to our railway ctin,tllssIon>
who have jurisdiction by legislatioP >
second, the government's subsidy plan; N^hiid, the! development and encouragement of tramp fehips and indirect aid to them in more freedoim of use of our ocean ports.	\
This particular method has been approved by the Interstate Commerce Conmissiom. The government are relying jgn the 'epfisfc of a special committee of	rega-ding
agricultural conditions, p^Bftfred to the House a few years ago. This cWnmittee was not appointed for the purpose raf dealing with oceaa rates. It was appointed \ to investigate agricultural conditions, but instead of staying in their own pond they wandefed away out into the lake and the ocean. I wisuld not call their rate "investigation" an investigation at all. True, they had prominent agriculturists appear and give evidence, but so far as my recollection goes only a few railway officials were called on the question of transportation and ocean rates. Yet to-day the government are basing their action in this matter on the report of that committee.
In contrast to that report let me call the attention of the House to the report on interstate, international, and ocean transportation of the commit! ee on Interstate Commerce of the United States. That committee summoned world-renowned rail and shipping experts, including Mr. Acworth, the British railway expert who jointly with Sir Henry Drayton, reported on Canada's railways. This report shows that competition on the ocean is the prime factor in regulating rates. For instance, before the opening of the Panama canal practically every large city and town of the United States was in rebellion against railway rates, but with the competition *which followed the opening of the Panama canal, the competition of rail versus water, the railways of that country were brought to time. I am sorry this voluminous, modem and practical report has not been quoted more frequently. The evidence goes to show that where there are competitive rates between all-parallel-water and all-rail traffic there is opportunity for regulating
Ocean Shipping Rates
transportation rates, but out on the ocean it is different. You cannot regulate the broad ocean like the land and especially when ships have a monopoly it is practically impossible to regulate ocean rates. The report is both pertinent and practical as a guide on this case in Canada. This report shows that what I say is correct and it is a good report.
I think this parliament should order a very careful inquiry. After all, a committee of this House, with all due respect to the House and to the committees, is not a proper forum to deal with such a problem. I differ from the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) in that regard; and I think I am borne out by the report of the Interstate Commerce Commission which investigated the economic side of the question, as to how these things affected the farmer, the manufacturer and the consumer. We can only obtain lower rates in my opinion by competition on the ocean on the basis of the law of supply and demand. The opening up of the St. Lawrence waterways, from the head of the Great Lakes, will do a great deal to stabilize matters in Canada along these lines. I have given three of the reasons which I have to offer. The fourth remedy for present conditions is the extension and better use of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine, and the fifth suggestion is to leave it to open competition and the free trade law of supply and demand, and to in time secure a reduction through education, negotiation and publicity, with all the cards on the table.
Coming from A large distributif.g centre in Central Canada, and as chairman of an inland port and harbour commission, I have been very much fnterested for many years in the question of ocean and lake transportation. The two things that I have wondered at at the outset] of this subsidy contract are: (1) why specifications were not prepared, and tenders were not called for, if the government has decided on the subsidy plan, and Canadian and English companies given a chance to tender, and the same principle adapted that applies to the gulf and sea ports regarding subsidies for mails and subventions of the Trade and Commerce department; and (2) why Sir William Petersen should be singled out for special favours in view of the fact that you had a contract with Sir William Petersen in 1897 and he treated it simply as a scrap of paper. Why was he singled out among all the different companies on the Atlantic and the Pacific? And why was a private tender given to him for this work? I think the government of Canada, after the
Ocean Shipping Rates

ernment's idea of rate regulation, tenders should have been called for on carefully drawn specifications. They should have been open to all and not been given without any competition whatever to Sir William Petersen, w'ho, as I say, treated his former contract as a scrap of paper. State aid to break a conference or combine will not solve the question. We have learned since the debate started that the committee can amend the contract and that the Canadian Pacific can come in second-hand on the same terms. What is this all going to cost, with this now free-for-all extension of the subsidy plan?
If ocean rates are too high, another effort should be made to secure control through the medium of a joint imperial board working as a unit. The re-creation of the subsidy plan is a relic of the mistakes made on land in Canada's extravagant railway subsidy policy. State aid by subsidy is no cure at all to lower lake and ocean rates. Canada would get better results either by building or by purchasing new ships for the merchant marine, with new and faster ships for the Atlantic and the re-routing of some of the present merchant marine vessels for Atlantic trade, than by giving 813,000,000 in a ten-year subsidy without competition. How can ten ships with fifty sailings a year control a thousand ships with fifty thousand sailings a year in a rate war? Canada's best interests would be better served by a spirit of cooperation with the British government in solving the problem, and by utilizing Canada's investment in railway facilities, merchant marine and other resources in unison with the British government. Canada learned in the war the good results that flowed from co-operation in shipping and trade and commerce with the British authorities.
Let us not forget that:
1.	The Petersen Company signed a somewhat similar contract with the Laurier government in 1897. It was unable to live up to the contract and it was cancelled.
2.	If the rates are so excessively high, why is the Canadian merchant marine losing $9,000,000 a year?
3.	Why did the United States Shipping Board lose $35,000,000 in the operation of 317 full vessels last year, with 913 inactive vessels?
4.	How can the Petersen line, with ten vessels, which at most can make only fifty voyages in a season between Montreal and Great Britain, break a combine, when in 1924 nine hundred and thirty-seven vessels cleared from the port of Montreal?
fMr. Church.]
5.	What is the need of subsidizing out of the treasury of the country an English line which has to build its ships when Canadian government-owned ships are rusting m Canadian haAours?
The west is not taking kindly to this measure, for I read in a western paper the other day a strong article opposed to it. The Progressives in this House have a fiscal organ of their own, the Grain Growers' Guide, and that journal has this to say on the subject:
W havre no more use for an ocean shipping combine than we have for any other kind of a combine, but when we have a government line of merchant ships and when the taxpayers have to make up the losses of that line every year to the tune of $9,000,000, because the ships cannot get cargoes to bring into this country, it is very apparent that it is not by subsidies to private shipping concerns that lower ocean rates are going to be secured. We could at least try the effect of lower rates on our own ships, and thus find out whether the lack of inward cargoes is due to high rates or the high rates are due to a lack of cargoes.
6.	Why not hold a proper inquiry under the direction of such a body as was constituted by the United States government to investigate a similar question? Before such a body you could take evidence and examine witneisses on a proper scale; you could call experts who would know something about ocean rates and water traffic generally.

In this case they did not apply within the two years, and therefore they have had

to come to parliament for that right. subtopic: WEST VIRGINIA PULP AND PAPER COMPANY
speechtext:
The Patent Act has definite provisions as to renewal of patents. Of course, if a man neglects those provisions and his patent dies he must go to parliament and parliament can either restore the patent or put him in the position of having to apply again on the merits, just as if no default had taken place. But I do not understand why one man should be relieved of the penalty of his default while another should not. I do not see any difference at all between this case and that presented the other night by the hon. member for St. Lawrenee-St. George. The rule that has been followed as long as I can remember is this:	If the applicant can
show special circumstances-for instance, that the instructions he left with his counsel were quite clear but through neglect or oversight, through something for which he was not himself responsible, his patent lapsed-then the practice has been to consider his peculiar position and relieve him of the penalty. Possibly the circumstances that I have revealed might"not be considered sufficient. The hon. member has not brought out any special circumstances in this case; the patentee simply lost his patent through neglect. While it is true we are only putting him back where he can apply again on the merits, still we are relieving him wholly of the default. What right has he to that?

subtopic: WEST VIRGINIA PULP AND PAPER COMPANY
speechtext:
I quite agree with the leader of the opposition in this matter. Two years ago we revised the Patent Act with great care; the discussion was as thorough as we have had on any statute in recent years. The question of patents is a highly technical and complicated matter. I recall that, if anything, the House leaned to the side of leniency to applicants; that we softened many of the provisions suggested by the Commissioner of Patents and, on the whole, we dealt very generously with the public in the matter. Now, as far as I can see-and I am speaking only from the knowledge I gained through an examination of the bill; I do not know the parties at all; I know nothing about it-here we have an American citizen who six years and a half ago allowed his rights under the patent to lapse. To-day he comes along and wants the rights granted him under the Patent Act extended. Now we propose by a special act to, as it were, wipe out the conditions of the main statute, the Patent Act, and place this man in a specially favoured position. I would say that certainly there is no rush about this thing. The man himself has allowed it to rest for six years. There must be some special reason why he now desires to revive the patent. It may be that some one has discovered or is trying to patent some process, or whatever it is that this covers, similar to this man's patent. It may be that someone else is very much more deserving than he is. It may be that in the evolution of the pulp and paper business this particular process or patent has a prospect of becoming more valuable, and therefore he desires to revive it, after he has allowed all these six years to elapse without protecting his rights.
I agree with what the hon. member for Lisgar said the other night, that certainly we have to give the discoverer of a process or device protection, but we give that protection under the Patent Act. After years and years of consideration in this country, and in other countries, we have come to the conclusion that a certain well defined period is justified and warranted, but this practice of coming back to the House and asking for the revival of some extinguished rights, which has been growing of late years, I think is a verj' dangerous practice.
What I would suggest to the House is this:	Let this thing stand. Let it go over
for a year. The gentleman who is asking for it allowed it to go for six years, and it is not going to hurt a particle to let it rest
Private Bills

for another year. We have just as much right to revive this patent next year as this, and in the interim the business, whatever it is that is affected by this, would have disclosed itself, as undoubtedly it will. I certainly object to blindly passing this bill without a very great deal more information than is before us at the present time, and particularly so-I do not know whether this is a reason, but still I advance it, not particularly as a reason, but rather as something to take note of-as we are asked to revive this patent for a gentleman by the name of Viggo Drewsen, of the city of Brooklyn, in the state of New York. I question very much, Mr. Chairman-indeed, I do not think there is any question about it, I venture to say-that a Canadian citizen under parallel circumstances would get short shrift in Washington. I doubt if he would get his application as far as the outer doors of the Capitol, and I doubt very much whether we are helping Canadians, in fact, the chances are we are depriving some Canadian of a parallel right, by resurrecting this extinguished right under the general Patent Act.
Mr. M.cGIVERIN:	I do not know anything more about it than as chairman of the committee all that we have done is to bring it before the commissioner. Mr. ANDREW McMASTER (Brome) moved the second reading of Bill No. 26, respecting a patent of Walter W. Williams.
He said:	Mr. Speaker, when a patentee
wishes to get letters patent in this country for an invention he has to make a payment of $15 on applying for his patent, and a further payment of $20 within six months of the date when the patent is issued to him. If he does not pay within the six months his patent is forfeited. Now, the petitioner in this private bill applied for a patent, and he paid $15 with his application. Then when the patent was issued to him he forgot to pay the other $20, the six months elapsed, and his patent became forfeited. Thereupon he applied1 under section 3 of the Patent Act, which reads as follows:
A forfeited application may be restored and the patent granted thereon on application to the commissioner within six months of the occurrence of the forfeiture, or the passage of this act, on payment with the application for restoration, in addition to the fee payable on the granting of the patent, of a further sum of $15.
He made his further payment of $15; then even before the patent was issued he made a further payment of $20. The patent was issued and the commissioner at least thought that everything was perfectly correct. But as this House has no doubt observed, lawyers sometimes differ, and a counsel who had to look into the validity of the patent raised the question, whether the patentee should not have paid the last $20 at the same time as he paid the $15. Now, I am inclined to think that that view is rather narrow and technical. The commissioner evidently thought so, because he allowed the patent to issue, the man having paid, prior to the issue of the patent, all the fees in connection therewith. But I can quite understand that a lawyer might read clause 3 to mean that when a patent was forfeited you had not only to pay the ordinary fee on the new application but also the fee on the new issue. I do not think that is really what parliament intended, but it is open to that construction. The patentee desires that his patent should be free from any possibility of doubt, and so he has asked for the passage of this act, which in effect says: Your patent is all right; it was issued to you properly; the commissioner's action was satisfactory in the premises. That is the object of the bill. There is this saving clause:
If any person has prior to the seventh day of February, 1925, commenced to construct, manufacture, use or sell in Canada the invention covered by the
said patent, such person may continue to construct, manufacture, use or sell the said invention in as full and ample a manner as if this act had not been passed.
I cannot see that any public or private interest is affected by this legislation. It is merely sought for the purpose of placing the validity of the patent beyond any doubt.
Would the hon. gentleman say what is the nature of the article patented?

It is a patent granted
for a liquid fuel atomizer.
What is that?
It is an atomizer used in connection with liquid fuel.

Mr. Speaker, here again we have a bill similar to a large number of -bills whidh have been introduced an recent years and affecting very seriously the issuing of patents. In this case, according to the statement of my hon. friend (Mr. McMaster), which I notice follows pretty closely the preamble, a gentleman comes to the House, through an hon. member, and asks that a special act be passed. To do what? To confirm a patent which the Commissioner of Patents has already issued, and which in his judgment-and his judgment should guide this House-is a perfectly valid patent under the statute. I am not a lawyer, and I ask my hon. friends who are lawyers not to judge my objection and suggestion too critically. In the last section of the bill we have what purports to be a saving clause. Now I submit this suggestion to the House, and I should like to have the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) give his opinion on it:	Would it not be possible
under this saving clause for the applicant to have made a secret arrangement regarding the manufacture of the article patented, and then later to sell the patent to some large firm, we will say to the Westinghouse Company, and within six months or a year afterwards for the party with whom he had made the secret arrangement to come forward and say, "Oh, but I manufactured the patented article during that hiatus, and under this clause I claim the right to continue the manufacture, although in the meantime the patentee has sold his patent to a bona fide purchaser?"
I am afraid the House may not be saving this gentleman from a loss or a possible loss, but rather creating a condition under which it is perhaps possible to defraud an innocent and honest purchaser of his patent. Bills of this character, which I discussed a moment

ago when the minister was not in his seat, directly affect a statute which (governs the whole intricate question of patent, and I do not think one of them should be brought before the House until it has been most carefully scrutinized, first by the Commissioner of Patents who is an expert, and his assistant, and secondly by the law officers of the crown. I think the public are entitled to that safeguard.
