subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN-MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the proposed resolution to ratify and confirm a contract between His Majesty and Sir William Petersen providing for the establishment of a subsidized steamship line on the Atlantic and government control of ocean rates and the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Clark.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN-MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext:
Ocean Shipping Rates

I believe in the freedom of the seas-for the merchant marine-as far as possible free from legislative control, and I think the history of Britain's merchant marine, and what it has done in its long and honourable history for shipping, trade and commerce, for humanity and the human race, and the oversea dominions-will justify my contention that it is entitled to fair treatment and not to be condemned hastily and that the government in trying the subsidy plan is seeking to accomplish the impossible.
I believe we should leave the whole question to the economic law of supply and demand, and as far as possible free of direct legislative control, which has not got us anywhere, even on the land, as a regulator of rates.
I believe it is neither desirable nor advisable or at all1 practicable to invest any external authority with power to fix rates for the ocean by arbitrary methods and compulsion; whereas negotiations, conferences and conciliation, education and publicity are in the long run better and more effective. The government's subsidy plan is virtually a declaration of war against the whole merchant marine, whom the Preston report criticizes and literally denounces as rate robbers. It is a declaration of martial law out on the ocean by mobilizing ten ships of the line to fight the conference. Such a toy fleet could not fight a combine or a conference on lake Ontario, let alone on the ocean, and it will lead to nowhere. I should like to quote an eminent authority regarding the folly of trying to regulate rates, whether by subsidy or by any other control of the sea. This empire came into being by the sea. It could not continue to exist without the sea. One of the most eminent authorities on the mercantile marine is Mr. E. Keble Chatterton, and he writes at page 244 of his new work, issued after the war, with regard to the folly of trying to interfere with the freedom of the seas. He says;
Thus, with glorious traditions behind them, and an equally glorious future in front, the mercantile marines of the nations of the maritime world have every reason to be proud of their respective services. Competition there assuredly will be, not merely between British and American, but, presently, German merchant fleets. That is all for the good of the services concerned and for the world in general. The lesson from past history is that maritime legislation in the long run is better omitted except where it is necessary as a reply to that of another country setting up unfair competition. The real freedom of the seas is to allow the merchant ship to pursue her way freely, unhampered; and to find her trade where she can, and be allowed to develop that trade as it has been in the past by Venetian, Spaniard, Dutch, Briton, American and others. To interfere with this system is to court trouble which in the long run fails to benefit the very organization it was intended to protect.

Navigation laws are all very well in intention; but far better still is it to allow free trading over the seas; free flow of emigrants and commerce, fair opportunities for all. The best must win in the last instance, but why not let each marine go about its own business as each trading concern ashore is allowed to carry on its own affairs? The merchant fleets mean too much to be controlled by the state in any country, except under exceptional circumstances and with the most weighty excuse. That is one of the lessons in the history of our subject, and we may leave it at that.
These are prophetic words used at the present time. The hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) was doubtful whether we could accomplish anything by rate regulation. Mr. Justice Mabee was of the same opinion, and the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) the other night said that there was no use in going any further in trying to regulate ocean rates. I might quote from other economic text book writers, but time will not permit.
The government is to be criticized for failure to aid in making the Canadian people a seagoing people and mariners. If we are ever to become or try to become a maritime people, we should attempt to turn out from our population a supply of merchant marine men. In the United States they are turning their war plants into peace plants, and they are building up a merchant marine fleet to go out over the seven seas of the world and capture the trade for the United States. In the United States this preparation for the sea is being carried out with that thoroughness which was shown during the war for making sailors out of raw landsmen. The recruiting for the American workers of marine, according to the latest official reports to hand, already consists of a personnel which is 68 per cent American. Its Sea Training Bureau has training stations and training ships, and in the first three yeara it turned out between 30,000 and 40,000 unlicensed ratings. In addition there are the navigation and engineering schools and advanced courses for men already holding licenses. Such subjects as the operation, repair, adjustment and general upkeep of marine turbines and matters dealing with electricity and oil, are included in the last-mentioned curricula. The result was that in four years licenses were granted to over 10,000 graduates as masters, first, second and third mates, chief engineers, first, second and third assistant engineers. By means of a sea service bureau maintained at various Atlantic, gulf and Pacific coast ports, during one year over 100,000 officers and men were placed in United States ships.
In my opinion the railway commission should be consulted in regard to this matter. We had an inquiry some years ago by the hon.

Ocean Shipping Rates
member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) and Mr. Acworth, and they say in their report presented to parliament in 1917 in connection with rates on land and ocean:
Railway policy is a sealed book to the ordinary citizen. Why tariffs should be fixed as they are. why the train service should not be arranged so as better to suit his individual requirements, why cars cannot always be available for everybody everywhere, he cannot understand The normal attitude of the public towards the railway management, whether in the hands of a company or a government, is one of mistrust, if not of active hostility. It is a good thing both for the railway itseif and for its patrons to bring the management out into the open; to have the reasons why such and such conditions exist, why certain concessions demanded cannot reasonably be granted, frankly explained in public.
The report goes on to refer to the ocean again and the principle of subsidies. It reads:
We think also that no subsidy or guarantee should be granted except after a similar report from the commission; and that no subsidy or guarantee should be voted in any session, unless it has been provided for in the financial budget of the year; and unless a substantial deposit of cash or securities has been made by the promoters, to prove the bona fides of their application.
That is a sound policy, and had Canada pursued that policy on land, for instance instead of three railways running along the north shore of lake Ontario where one railway with a double track would have been sufficient, only one line would have been constructed, and a waste of money which amounts to about a billion dollars would have been prevented. What has been done on the land can be done on the ocean.
The subsidy principle will benefit neither the producer, nor the farmer, nor the shipper, nor the grain grower, nor the manufacturer. It benefits simply one ship-owner at the expense of all the others. It benefits also the middleman. If the object is to assist the producer, the farmer, the grain grower, or the raiser of cattle, it would be better to bonus that industry. This would go directly to the farmer. Otherwise the farmer secures no direct benefit from this subsidy.
I was going to say something about how the tramp ships succeeded to the carrying trade, the tramp steamer as a factor in carrying goods and in the regulation of rates, and the creation of liners and their effect on higher rates. To-day the finest merchant ships in the world are not freighters, but passenger ships. It is the tramp which has succeeded to the carrying trade of those pioneer ships; and after the Indian monopoly had disappeared, and there came a need for people to go to the East, it was quite an innovation to provide more accommodation for passengers. Then the same thing happened in regard to China, but especially with the emigration to Australia.
88i
Gradually this element increased and again people began to travel all over the world, for business, for administrative reasons, for pleasure ; and as the number of passengers increased, so the amount of cargo space was encroached upon. Especially was this the case in the transAtlantic ships, so that to-day the principal liners on that route carry practically no cargo beyond mails and the passengers' luggage. Thus, within a hundred years, the needs of the public have entirely altered the character of the shipping.
It was natural enough that the East should for so long have instigated all the improvements in shipping for the reason that travellers went to the Orient long before America was discovered, and the East India Company had a continuous need for the best ships. But since the introduction of steam and the rapid progress of the United States, it is the West, and not the East which has always seen the greatest enterprise in shipping. Bigger and better vessels, compound engines, twin screws, triple screws, quadruple screws, turbines, oil fuel, increased speed, luxurious accommodation-all these most important and progressive factors in the mercantile marine have come as a result of the Atlantic, and not the oriental trade. These reflect, as everybody knows, on the rates, the high cost of ocean travel and so forth. If this subsidy goes through, you may be in a British port and you may see one or two of these ten ships of the line under subsidy at a dock. At the next dock you will see a tramp ship, and the tramp ship will have quite a grievance against the state-owned ship, subsidized as it is, and against the citizens of Canada for helping to pay for and maintain that ship over there. Such a policy will interfere with free competition for the tramp ship, because the tramp ship, as the evidence showed before the Interstate Commerce Commission, is one of the most important factors in rate regulating. This policy of subsidizing ships may drive tramp ships out of business; it may drive some of them to the wall.
In my opinion the subsidizing of these ten steamships under the present contract will strike a decided blow at the free competition which exists ordinarily with the operation of tramp ships. And according to the text book writers, the owner of tramp vessels is to-day a public benefactor; indeed, the tramp ship-owner is a greater benefactor than Sir William Petersen would ever be, even though the latter may be state-aided. The tramp ship gets no bonus or subsidy but it proves an important factor in our Canadian trade. In 1921 there were 301 tramps from

Ocean Shipping Rates
Montreal; in 1922, 409; in 1923, 246 and last year 447. As an hon. member has pointed out, some 153,000,000 bushels of grain were carried out of the port of Montreal in the past year, of which tramp steamers carried 60 per cent. We had a case in Toronto of both rail and rail and water rates quoted by the railways from Toronto to Vancouver on package freight. A tramp ship obtained from the Canadian merchant marine was bought by the Kirwood line and it set a cheap all water rate from Toronto to Vancouver 'via the Panama canal; it cut the rates materially and saved the merchants in Toronto a lot of money.
The government's policy will so hamper the freedom of tramp steamers as to remove competition in the open market for freight. In other words, the government will bonus the tramp's competitor, taking away a part of his customers. Now, the tramp ship has an important function to perform, and if hon. gentlemen will only consult the figures for any ocean, gulf or lake port in Canada they will see what an important factor the tramp steamer has been in Canadian shipping. Let us. beware of this policy; we do not want to do anything that will eliminate competition. Let us ensure regular business for the tramp steamers and in that way maintain competition. The regular liner has a different function to perform from that of the tramp, for the liner's sailings are always advertised in advance. The liner takes its business in a different way from the tramp and often confines its traffic to one point.
All these things must be borne in mind. I do not think that any hon. gentleman in this House can have any doubt in his mind as to what effect this contract will have on the tramp steamers. The hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean) and the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) have both expressed on this subject views to which I must take exception, namely, favouring the co-ordination of the Canadian National and Canadian Pacific Railways. Let me say emphatically here that it is not public ownership that has got our railways into their present condition, but private ownership. I do not believe in the policy which these hon. gentlemen have enunciated, for it strikes me as being-another way only of handing over the Canadian National railways to the Canadian Pacific Railway, which is the very thing that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company wants to brifrg about. Competition is the life of trade, and there is every reason why we should encourage competition between the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian National

system. I am sorry that the hon. member for South York, the dean of the House a public ownership man, is not here to-night, because I should like to say to him that the policy he advances will not prove a solution of the problem we have to cope with. What is suggested would only create a vaster combine than has so far existed.
It is my firm belief that a measure of such supreme importance, before being adopted by this parliament, should be submitted to the people for their approval or otherwise. I certainly do not think that we should undertake at this time to endorse it. It seems to me that we stand in the greatest need of a control of rates, not only as they affect ocean transportation but also as they apply to our railways. There is no doubt whatever in my mind that a combine exists in the passenger associations of the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific, and that combine meets to fix rates to suit itself. Let us realize once and for all that it is not only on the ocean that a conference dictates the rates that shall be charged; [DOT] there is a conference on the land as well known as an association, and it is as bad as the Atlantic combine on the ocean. The representatives of our two great railway systems sit around a table and fix rates, and both of them have an eastern and a western passenger association. These two railways utterly ignore the Board of Railway Commissioners, and this has been proved to be the case. It seems to me that if the Canadian National Railways were really anxious to secure the cream of the passenger traffic from the large centres of population, they would adopt the system that prevails in connection with the railways in Great Britain, Australia, France and in the United States;
that is to say, they would give to 9 p.m. the working people who are paying the taxes something in return for their money, in the form of reduced rates for week-end holidays, fall fairs, conventions and similar occasions. This would enable the working classes to get out of the large and congested cities into the country and so have some chance of building up their health, instead of living in close tenement houses. Let me inform the House that the British railways have found these cut rates on special occasions to make good business. But what are our National Railways doing? They simply sit around a table with the Canadian Pacific Railway, and when the representatives of that railway suggest a rate as their policy, the Canadian National says, "Me too". That is their policy-"Me too". Would it not be infinitely better for the Canadian National

Ocean Shipping Bates
Railways, by means of reduced rates on such special occasions to have their trains filled going out of Toronto, Hamilton and other large centres, instead of as at present with hardly anyone on them? Let them cut their rates and in that way obtain the cream of the passenger business. Talk about a combine on the Atlantic! Why, a greater combine for the fixing of rates exists in connection with railway transportation in this country and this in face of the fact that a railway commission is supposed to exercise of their own volition some oversight in railway matters. During the last two years the railway commission might be described as lost, strayed or stolen, so far as any influence it has exerted is concerned. For all the good it has done recently it might as well be abolished, and it seems to me that if railway rates cannot be regulated within the four comers of Canada on land there is not much hope of success when the government undertakes to apply control of rates on gulf, lake and river, and even on the ocean. If this subsidy policy is extended it will cost the country a great deal * more than $13,000,000 in ten years. If, as the Prime Minister has suggested, an offer is made to other concerns, say the Canadian Pacific Steamship Company, and they come in on the same basis, and if others also come in on the same basis, where is this thing going to end? Nobody knows what it will cost. The farmers do not know; this House does not know. It may be analogous to the case of the Grand Trunk and the Grand Trunk Pacific where years ago it was stated that the cost to the country would be $14,000,000, but the hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) showed the other night that up to date the cost had been over half a billion -and we are not through with it yet. More than that, the deficit on operation of the National railways is sixty or seventy millions a year; and this is nothing but an added subsidy put into the taxes for the boon of free competition between the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National.
The British authorities, who have done so much for Canada in maritime matters are very much alarmed about this proposal. So moderate a paper as the Morning Post, of London, England, a very conservative organ says:
In this country the ipriraciple of subsidizing shipping is considered to be unsound. It tends to relaxation of effort on the part of the subsidized. Moreover, that one province of the empire should confer an advantage by means of a state subsidy upon one particular line of steamships is to interfere with the unity of the shipping services of the Empire. It is to the profit of every part of the empire that sea transport should be conducted upon a common policy, in which the interests alike of shippers, passengers, and
ship owners are impartially and fairly recognized. And the British shipping industry may justly claim that it has been, and is being, conducted upon that principle. It was built up by individual enterprise, without state assistance other than payment for the carriage of mails or retaining fee for the use of vessels in war; and at a time when shipbuilding is three and four times what it was before the war, and the cost of management double and treble, British ship owners continue to conduct their business without asking anything from the government except freedom from regulations which would place them at a disadvantage as compared with the foreigner. The duration of the contract made by the Canadian government is stated to be ten years. It may be doubted if it will last quite as long.
I doubt it, too. The last contract in 1897 with Sir William Petersen lasted less than a year, and then Sir William Petersen was handed back his money with interest in 1899. I quote from another despatch from Great Britain, dated at London, February 16:
Sir Halford MacKinder, chairman of the Imperial Shipping Committee, the body erected by the Imperial Economic conference of 1923 to consider disputes, writes a complaining letter in to-day's Times. He says several of the complaints made by W. T. R. Preston were not first presented to the Imperial Committee and that two favourable reports on other Canadian complaints were made by the committee and two more are in preparation. Hon. Mackenzie King voted for the creation of this committee, which he now disregards.
The idea is growing in England that Preston's report, much of which is characterized by the Atlantic Conference as wild and unfounded, is only a step in a political move by Premier King. The Morning Post, devotes a column to this thesis.	.
Meantime the rumour persists that the Canadian-Pacific will jump out of the conference and accept the Canadian government's subsidy to avoid the competition of rival lines to Canadian ports, consequent upon the reduction of the United States quota. The handing to the Canadian Pacific Railway of immigrants now sent by the Cunard and White Star lines, as well as those by the Dutch and Scandinavian lines, would mean big business to the Canadian Pacific Railway, especially in view of the attempt of the Liberal government shortly to be made to increase Canada's waning population by indiscriminate recruiting on the continent of Europe.
That is what the chairman of the Imperial Shipping committee says. Then, in the British House of Commons the other day, on the orders of the day, the Parliamentary Secretary of the Board of Trade, Sir B. Chadwick, in reply to Mr. B. Smith, socialist, Rotherhithe, who asked whether there was a great disparity in the freight rates to Canada for settlers' effects charged by conference lines and non-conference lines, said that the whole question of trade rates would shortly be investigated by a special parliamentary committee in Canada. I quote from a report in the Morning Post:
Mr. B. Smith asked whether, in accordance with the Preston report, which was a Canadian government official report, that colony intended to treat the favouritism between Germany and other countries as against British exports and imports to Canada as a first-class political issue, having regard to the fact
Ocean Shipping Rates

Ocean Shipping Rates
sat in with the Canada Steamships to fix the same high rates instead of allowing free and impartial competition to give relief.
High rates are not confined to the ocean. We have in this country high telephone rates, high express rates, high telegraph rates, high railway rates. The railway commission virtually allows all these public service corporations to do what they please. We have high sales taxes and high income taxes. How is it that this is the only combine that is attacked? What about all these other combines on land that we have in this country-the bread combine, the oil combine, the bankers' combine, the American millionaires' combine grabbing our resources, the gasoline combine, the grain growers' combine, the coal combine, the elevator combine, the transportation combine and the manufacturers' combine? We have a Combines Act, passed in 1923, but how many prosecutions have ever been made under it? Not one. How many prosecutions have been made under the criminal code with regard to restraint of trade? None. We tried to get a bill of indictment a few years ago against the milk industry in Toronto, at a time when there were a lot of people out of work and the rates for milk were raised unduly. We also attacked the bread and restaurant combines. We said there was a combine of the milk association that met and fixed prices and we presented a bill of indictment to a judge at the Toronto assizes but could get nowhere. Trusts and combines are flourishing like a green bay tree in this country from coast to coast. They can regulate them in England and the United States but we cannot do it here. Yet the government ignores these land combines to interfere with the law of supply and demand on the ocean. They do not attack the trusts and combines within the confines of Canada where they have jurisdiction. Charity should begin at home instead of away out on the ocean, where we have no jurisdiction. We should first deal with the combines at home. The Imperial Shipping Board is to meet in the Old Country in a few days and take evidence. A new investigation has been ordered in England into the whole ocean rate problem in view of Canada's action.
In conclusion, I want to say a word on behalf of the party of which I am a humble member. It has been charged in this House, and in a number of party papers, including some Progressive papers, and we heard a great deal of talk also along the same line during the last election, that this party is allied with the big interests in this country. The Prime Minister and the Minister of
Labour-I am not criticizing them particularly-have referred to us as the party supporting the big interests. Last session When legislation was brought down with reference to the agricultural implement industry, it was charged that this party represented the agricultural implement industry of this country. That is not so. In the Ontario election, the agricultural implement industry did its best to keep the Drury government in power. The Conservatives are not the allies of the big interests and of the agricultural implement manufacturers. I can speak not only for myself but I think for the whole Conservative party when I say that we serve no big interests. Some of us have suffered in the battle against the big interests and are prepared to suffer again. We have battled against them in Toronto, to give that city freedom from combines in light, transportation and power. Conditions were such that only a rich man could afford to have electricity in his house, because it was costing from two to three dollars per unit for light and power. But to-day every workman in the city of Toronto has electric light in his home at a cost of 92 cents per unit as compared with two or three dollars a few years ago. So I say the Conservative party represent no big interests. On the contrary, we have battled against them, and are prepared to do so again. While we criticize this policy of the government we desire, and I believe every member of this House desires, to see lower rates on the ocean and on the lakes as well. I agree with the object the government is seeking to attain, but I disagree with the method they propose to accomplish that object. For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I am opposed to the proposed Petersen agreement.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN-MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had hoped during the progress of this debate that some substantial reason would be advanced by the government, or by some member on the opposite side of the House, to show why we should support this resolution; but instead of that, we have had various explanations regarding the issue that is before us, and most of them have been to the effect, in my judgment at least, that the subject matter of this resolution is not really before the House at all, but something else. That would be especially true, I think, of the explanation made by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Marler) this afternoon.
But let us take just the first three lines of the resolution:
Resolved, that to give the government of Canada control over certain ocean rates it is expedient to

with respect to operating costs which would seem to bear out the essential claim of Sir William, although neither has included anything for what may be called " managerial expenses." I should hardly think, however, this would t>e a very large item as our own shipping officers and freight solicitors on this side could canvass freight for the new proposition as well a3 the railway without additional expense.
There is a clause in the agreement to the effect that they will co-operate with the Canadian Government Merchant Marine and the Canadian National Railways. I contend that that clause is not really a provision to guard the interests of the National Railways, but it is really a clause that gives something to Sir William Petersen, or compels him apparently to go into a relation which would be of very great advantage to himself. I submit that it may be of some value to the Canadian National Railways to get ten modern ships, or ships possibly 'better than the ones they have, if they really are, some advantage for the National Railways to have some improvement in the steamship service in direct connection with the railway; but when it comes to the other side of the bargain, when we consider the advantage to Petersen, in addition to the subsidy, of being linked up with the Canadian National Railways, there is absolutely no comparison between .the advantage of Sir William Petersen and the advantage to the Canadian National Railways. The advantage to Sir William Petersen is overwhelming, and the advantage to the Canadian National Railways is almost nothing. The things are not on a parity; there is no comparison. So that that clause in my opinion is of very little value so far as the country is concerned.
There is another matter I wish to refer to, and that is that we have at present the Canadian Government Merchant Marine, and we have in the north Atlantic apparently a surplus tonnage, and this policy calls for an addition to surplus tonnage. Does that not mean that the Canadian Government Merchant Marine will have proportionately less chance to get full cargoes than they have at the present time, and so increase the difficulty of earning dividends or getting return cargoes? That is the great difficulty, according to Sir Henry Thornton, in the way of making them pay. Why are we seeking to follow this policy of putting additional tonnage on the north Atlantic? But suppose these ships are a great improvement on the present Canadian Government Merchant Marine boats? The right hon. leader of the opposition claims that these boats are not necessarily an improvement. I think possibly in most respects they are not, but there seems to be one feature in which there is just a little improvement, 
and that is the proportion of net tonnage of the boats to the gross tonnage. Most of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine boats have a tonnage running about five thousand and over gross, and a net tonnage less than thirty-five hundred, while the Petersen boats have a gross tonnage of five thousand with a net tonnage of thirty-five hundred. There is not very much difference. But in any case if the government and Sir William Petersen are fitting those ships up to efficiently serve the trade in the north Atlantic, surely they have been collaborating together in order that we may get suitable boats, and drawing from the experience that has been gained from the operation of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine, they will be able thereby to judge more accurately the needs of the trade; and if these boats are better and practically brought into the Canadian National service, are we not going to turn to Petersen the profitable end of the shipping business, and hold for ourselves the less profitable end, the Canadian Government Merchant Marine, if that merchant marine is as unsuitable as has been claimed. And I do not therefore see why Petersen should be brought into this bargain at all. Petersen can get his subsidy, but what guarantee has the government of Canada or the Parliament of Canada that this business is going to be extended? What knowledge are they going to obtain of the business by handing a subsidy to Sir William Petersen? I submit the Canadian government and the merchant marine can operate boats as successfully as Sir William Petersen, and if they can do so and if the boats are profitable and successful, we will have the same access to knowledge of the shipping business as carried on by the new boats, as we now have with the Canadian Government Merchant Marine. But if the profitable end of our business is to be in private hands and the private company is to obtain all the advantage of being connected with a national system of railways, and all the advantages that the Canadian National can give them in the way of soliciting freight, I say we are letting business that ought to be in our hands get into the hands of private owners, and the government will be in this position, that seeking to fix reasonable rates they will not have access to the accounts and therefore will not have a proper knowledge of what the rates ought to be.
For a few moments I wish to examine some of the reasons that have been given as to why wre do not use the Canadian Government Merchant Marine. The right hon. leader of the opposition referred yesterday to the statement of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. MARCH 20, 1925
Ocean Shipping Rates
Motherwell) who said that the ships were too small for the ocean and too large for the lakes. When I heard that statement I could not help thinking of the old explanation of why men do not marry. The explanation was that young- men are too young and old men are too old. I think that matter was dealt with sufficiently yesterday, and there is no object in referring to it again. The hon. member for Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) went into another explanation. He stated at page 1070 of Hansard :
The Canadian Government Merchant Marine ships are of very different construction and, with the engines they have, in very rough weather cannot make more than five knots actual speed.
Then he said regarding the Petersen boats:
You will find that with the Diesel engines with which these ships will be equipped, they will be able to make their eleven knots at any time except, of course, in a very heavy gale of wind.
That is not a very good explanation, because it gives the speed of the merchant marine in very rough weather, and gives the speed of the new boats in fairly good weather. Perhaps the hon. member was canny in that regard. But in any case what is it that very largely determines the speed of a ship? Is it not the ratio of power to tonnage? You will find, if you examine the specifications of the Petersen boats, the 9,000 deadweight ton boats, or 5,000 gross tons, have an indicated horse-power of 2,250 and a brake horse-power of 1,850, while the boats of approximately the *same size in the merchant marine have an indicated horse-power of 3,000 and up to 4,000 with a brake horse-power of about 80 per cent of the indicated horse-power. Therefore, there is no reason for concluding, as far as I can see, that the Petersen boats with less horsepower in proportion to their weight, can have any greater speed, especially in rough weather, than the present boats of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine.
The Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham), gave us in his speech as the reason that the merchant marine boats could not be used, that they were at present in use and could not be switched to the north Atlantic. I am not very -well convinced that this is a good argument, because wherever you read about shipping to-day, there is a surplus tonnage everywhere and it would not appear that with a surplus tonnage throughout the world to the extent of millions of tons, there would be any great disturbance of trade on any route by the transfer of a few boats. But in any case, as I have argued before, there is no reason why we should hand over these boats to Sir William Petersen when we might utilize them
and do the same business as Sir William Petersen can do, the only difference being that in the one case we have to pay a subsidy without an actual knowledge of -the returns and, in the other, we would pay any deficit, if there was a deficit, with the fullest knowledge of the transaction. Sir Henry Thornton, speaking before the select standing committee on National Railways and Shipping last year was asked this question:
Q. Would you say this particular fleet we have now, of sixty vessels-has it any possibility of ever arriving at that condition? You spoke of the Canadian Pacific Railway? They have different kind of vessels? -A. Yes.
Q. Is it possible to secure success, in your opinion, with vessels we have now, or will it be a continual loss from year to year?-A. I would not like to make a positive assertion, but I will say this, somewhat tentatively; that, considering our merchant marine as a whole, we have to go either forward or backward. If we feel that the merchant marine service has a value to the people of Canada in all of their industrial activities, and to the railway itself, I think I should answer that question in the affirmative. Then we have to face up to, I think, putting these vessels, these implements in such shape as to get the maximum efficiency out of them.
There is just one other quotation I wish to read here, and that is with regard to the north Atlantic business. Sir Henry Thornton was asked this question:
Q. These returns are not very encouraging. You must have something to offset them?-A. Probably not to the United Kingdom, because if I remember the figures rightly, our total United Kingdom trade showed a deficit of about half a million dollars.
A little further on Sir Henry Thornton said:
We do not show any profit to the United Kingdom, and we can charge all of that to the wretched condition of the westbound movement.
I am opposed to this method of attempted control which, in my judgment, will not control at all, or at least I am not convinced that it is leading us in that direction. I am opposed to the resolution because I believe it is a step backwards and not the step forward that the man whom we have put in charge of the National railways and merchant marine has said that we should take. We are taking a backward step. I am opposed to the resolution because it is definite and specific with regard to this agreement, I am opposed to subsidies in general, and I am opposed to this one in particular until I get more information. If I am forced To vote on this question without additional information, I must vote against the resolution. I am opposed to it, in addition, because I believe we are not standing in the way of the measure of control that we could get through putting on additional boats, because we have the unit of organization now in the merchant marine,

I have in my hand the report of the Imperial conference of 1923, and it refers to the nugatory character of the recommendations of the Dominions Royal Commission. Nothing was done as a result of the investigation of the royal commission. I find that when the report which Sir Halford Mackinder presented to the Imperial conference, the most they had to recommend was that, instead of carrying on under the old system of deferred rebates that had 'been repudiated by a few of the dominions, they recommended a general application of the agreement system whereby shippers agreed to ship by conference lines. So, with the Imperial Shipping Committee coming up nearly to that point, in 1923 a point that South Africa had reached before by legislating against deferred rebates and recommending, instead agreements, I fear that the Imperial Shipping Committee, which apparently would be the body that would take this into consideration, would not give us results in time to save the cattle industry or any other industry that is in a very difficult position at this time. So, while I do not want to shut out this question, I am not willing at this stage to support the resolution as it stands. I shall, therefore, vote against the resolution if it is pressed to a vote in its present form, and I shall also vote against the amendment.

I got them this afternoon and I think it is only fair and just that they should be placed on Hansard. The first petition is from the Montreal Corn . Exchange Association, addressed to the House in the usual form, humbly showing:
That the question of ocean shipping is a complex and difficult one, and has been investigated by the very best authorities for many years; -
That the conclusions of these various investigations have not been unanimous; -
That any drastic legislative action concerning ocean transportation is 'fraught with the gravest danger, and should be based on a report made by a properly constituted commission with the fullest possible powers to thoroughly investigate all phases of this most involved question, as well as to closely analyse all reports issued by various commissions, committees and individuals regarding it; -
Wherefore, the committee of management of the Montreal Corn Exchange Association earnestly prays your honourable House not to ratify the proposed contract between the Dominion government and Sir William Petersen for the establishment and operation of a regular steamship service between Canadian ports and British and continental ports.
And your petitioners as in duty bound will ever pray, et cetera.
I at once assure the Prime Minister that the petition is duly signed both by the president and by the secretary of the association. The other petition is from the Montreal Board of Trade and reads :
That the government of Canada has contracted, subject to the ratification of the Dominion parliament, with one. Sir William Petersen, or a company to be formed by him, for the establishment and operation of a regular steamship service between Canadian ports and British and continental ports, the consideration for said service being an annual subsidy to be paid by the government, amounting to approximately $1,340,000, on the basis of a service of ten ships, the government having the right to demand that the service be doubled, in which case the subsidy will be increased proportionately; -
That the reasons adduced by the government for entering into the contract are that trading communities and interests of the country are seriously handicapped in their overseas trade by disadvantages artificially created by the indiscriminate and uncertain rates and conditions enforced by shipping combines or conferences, the existence of which combines or conferences, however, together with the disadvantages for which they are held responsible, seem to have been predicated largely on the report of an individual investigator, who, however sincere, did not possess the necessary authority or technical knowledge to conduct an investigation into a question which is international in its scope and character;-
That, it is impossible to influence ocean rates generally by the method proposed because it provides lower rates on a small part of the traffic only, saich lower rates benefiting only those shippers whose goods are carried by ships operating under the contract, and that at the cost of the already overburdened taxpayer; - That the expenditure of such a large sum annually as is called for under the contract cannot but be
contemplated with alarm, in view of the state of the national finances; -
Wherefore, the council of the Montreal Board of Trade earnestly prays your honourable House not to approve of the proposed contract, which would involve the country in such a heavy annual outlay without commensurate benefits to the citizens of Canada.
And your petitioners, as in duty bound, will ever pray, et cetera.
That petition also is duly signed by the president and the secretary of the board.

speechtext:
There are
evasions sometimes that work and evasions sometimes that recoil on themselves, and I am inclined to think that my hon. friend will find that most people are of the opinion that the English language means just what it says. The hon. gentleman says that what the government proposes to do in appointing a committee to investigate the matter is just what is asked in these petitions. That is not so. These petitions say definitely:	"Don't have
anything to do with the contract; don't overburden the tax-payer who already has a heavier load than he can carry. Don't do something ridiculous, something that will cope with only a very small modicum of the traffic, something that will have absolutely no effect on any general reduction of rates but will mean a tremendous expense to the rate-
10	p.m. payers". I have tried to be as brief as possible, Mr. Speaker, because I do not desire to delay hon. gentlemen who have made arrangements which they are bound to keep.
Mr. JEAN J. DENIS (Joliette):	I have
only a few words to say on the resolution but before casting my vote I should like to make my position clear and explain to the House my view of the question. What is sought in this proposed legislation is a reduction of ocean freight rates; and of all the problems which might come before the Parliament of Canada at any time there is none more arduous or more difficult than the problem of attempting to reduce the cost of ocean transportation. I say, therefore, at the very outset that any government that has the courage to try in any way to tackle this question and to wrestle with it ought to deserve the sympathy of the community at large as well as of hon. members of this House. I think we are all agreed that the reduction of freight rates, whether on land or on sea, is absolutely necessary in the interests of this country. Since the war freight rates have increased enormously, and this increase has
Ocean Shipping Rates

to a very large extent hampered the trade and the industrial development of Canada,
It is all very well to say we have an enormous country with unlimited resources, but those resources have to be carried to the markets of the world and unless we are able to carry them under conditions profitable to the growers, to the producers, to the miners, these magnificent resources can be of no avail. Therefore the government should be praised for their worthy attempt to reduce freight rates. Any such reduction would benefit all classes, more particularly the farmers; and in that connection I cannot forget the farmers of my own province, the old historic province of Quebec. I know wrhat hardships the farmers of my province are facing now and have been facing since the conclusion of the war. Only through their thrift, their industry, their endurance and their patience have they been able to cope with the situation brought about not through the fault of any government but on account of circumstances arising out of the war and post-war conditions. I know that the farmers not only of my province but of every province of this Dominion are anxious that freight rates should be reduced; and this applies also, as I have just said, to all other classes of the community. That being the case; everyone being anxious to see the rates reduced-and that has been the desire not this year only, but for many years, as was mentioned this afternoon-the government have made a move; they have come to parliament with a contract. They have asked parliament to examine that contract and to pass judgment upon it, not as it is set forth in the resolution, but as subsequently submitted by the committee of parliament to which the matter is to be referred. What is now being submitted to us, unless I am mistaken, is not a final, irrevocable proposition; it is a draft contract; and I base my opinion as to that on the declarations made by the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Low) and the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King).
I do not desire to pass judgment upon the procedure of this House, Mr. Speaker, but it would appear to me that the opposition have opposed the resolution altogether too soon. What was asked was merely the reference of the resolution to a committee for examination and investigation, and that being the case every hon. member might very well reserve his final judgment, as I intend to do, until the special committee reports back to the House. Unless I am greatly mistaken, the fate of this scheme will not be finally determined until the report of that 
committee is presented and until a vote of the House either gives effect to the contract or nullifies it. It seems to me, therefore, that it would have been much more appropriate to have deferred the discussion on the subject until after the committee had brought in their report. But hon. members on the other side were so anxious to engage in combat that they attacked the resolution immediately upon its being introduced and brought all their arguments to bear against it. For my part I do not intend to-night to discuss the merits of the resolution, except to say that on the face of it, it appears to me to be a worthy attempt on the part of the government to give the people of this country cheaper freight rates on the ocean. Is the resolution perfect? Are there any flaws in it? Can it be made better? All these questions will be submitted to the committee, and after the committee has made its report it will be time for us to judge as to the merits or demerits of the contract.
It appears to me that in following this procedure the government have not only acted in good faith but have also proceeded in a most democratic way. The autocratic method would have been to submit the contract to parliament and ask for a decision at once on the contract as submitted. The democratic way is to have the contract sent to a committee to be thoroughly examined, thoroughly sifted, thoroughly tested, and then for parliament to make its final decision when the report is brought in.
I listened this afternoon with a great deal of pleasure to the speech delivered by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Marler) and I must say that I am fully in accord with what he said. I wrote down one of his sentences as correctly as I could, and if I made no mistake it would read like this; "I reserve my attitude and my vote until the bill comes back from the committee." This is the stand I intend to take, Mr. Speaker. In accord with the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George I think that all hon. members who are anxious that ocean freight rates be reduced should give this resolution an opportunity to be discussed in committee; should have this question, so important to all classes of the country, fully gone into both in the committee and in the House when the report of the committee is presented. For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I will vote with pleasure for the resolution.
Mr. T. W. BIRD (Nelson); Mr. Speaker, after listening to most of this debate I have concluded that the only sensible thing to

Ocean Shipping Rates
do is to allow this proposal to go to a special committee. We are told that it would be a breach of parliamentary technique to vote for this resolution simply to enable the matter to be referred to a committee. Well, all I can say if technique stands in the way of the only sensible course to be taken, then so much the worse for the technique. I believe that the method of discussing trade resolutions prior to the introduction of a bill is something of a nuisance. It has involved us in a lot of waste time this week; in fact, we have wasted a whole week of parliamentary time over what is after all only a relic of procedure that has outlived its usefulness. I cannot see where there is any place in reason for discussion of this kind which leads to no practical results. I doubt whether in voting for this resolution we are transgressing, those of us who may ultimately be opposed to the final proposal, the technicalities of parliament. I believe it has been customary in the practice of this House to qse this stage of the discussion on a proposal of this kind to settle the general principle involved. I think that is all that has ever been expected from this stage of the discussion. Now I notice that the general question, the underlying principle, has been accepted in an almost unqualified way by almost all sides of this House, and yet we have wasted almost a week over that one particular. The general question of the desirability of the control of ocean freight rates has been almost universally accepted by this House.
I shall not try to delve into the motives of the government or of the Prime Minister in introducing the motion as they have. The official opposition attributed it to the desire of the Prime Minister to wriggle out of- I think that was the word used-the responsibility which is supposed to attach to the Prime Minister and his government. As I say, I do not know what the motive of the Prime Minister was. I do not care very much, although I desire to credit him with the best of motives. But whatever his motives were, I think his action in submitting this motion to the House with the proviso that it is only the general principle which is to be decided upon is to be commended in itself. I think it is in full accord with the tendencies of parliaments in modern times. The circumstances under which governments of old came down to the House with a policy in one hand, and a big stick in the other, fortunately are of the past. I think this ought to be dwelt upon a little. I think it is significant in these days that prime ministers do consult the wishes of the people, and the wishes of the representatives of the
people. To illustrate my point I want to refer to what I consider to be one of the most significant parliamentary incidents of modern times. I refer to the debate in the British House on the Trades Union Levy Amendment Bill. You will remember that the Conservative government in Great Britain came into power with the avowed policy of destroying the trades union political levy. That was their declared policy, but in the debate the other day on that proposition. Mr. Baldwin made history. He delivered a speech the like of which I venture to say has not been equalled in the British House. This is what the Manchester Guardian says of Mr. Baldwin's effort. After criticizing the old way of doing things that is, the big stick method of government, in which the government comes down to the House and says- take it or leave it-the Guardian goes on to say:
Mr. Baldwin's way was different. He made no promises about fulfilling his pledges later on when he had time to remember them; no threats against the recalcitrant members of his own .party; no impassioned pleas for the due observance of parliamentary procedure. " We abandon what we have laid our hands to," he said. " We, at any rate, are not going to fire the first shot. We stand for peace and to remove suspicion in the country. We want to create a new atmosphere in a new parliament for a new age in which the people can come together."
Then the editorial goes on to say:
If he (Mr. Baldwin) lives up to the spirit of this speech he will be a great Prime Minister. It was the speech of one, who though the leader of a great party and a great majority tries to interpret the will of the people irrespective of party, who would rather conciliate than dominate, who can look at the other fellow's point of view, and who does not forget that a Prime Minister owes more to his country than to his party. Whether so striking, so emphatic, and so unusual an appeal to idealism in party politics will meet with a fitting response from either his supporters or his critics remains to be seen. But we may be grateful that the appeal has been made.
Mr. Speaker, I will not be trespassing very much on the time of the House if I read one of the closing paragraphs of that wonderful speech. In the Manchester Guardian of the 7th of March the debate in the British parliament is given in full. I will read the second to the last paragraph of the speech:
We have our majority-
Hon. gentleman to my right ought to pay attention to this. This is a speech of a famous Tory leader:
We have our majority, we believe in the justice of this bill which has been brought in to-day, but we are going to withdraw to one side, and we are not going to push our political advantage home at a moment like this. We at any rate are not going to fire the first shot. We stand for peace. We stand for the removal of suspicion in the country. We want to create an atmosphere, a new atmosphere in a new
Ocean Shipping Rates

parliament, for a new age in which the people can come together. We abandon what we have laid our hands to. We know we may be called cowards for doing it. We know we may be told that we have gone back on our (principles. But at this moment we believe we know what the country wants, and we believe it is for us in our strength to do what no other party can do at this moment, and to say that we at any rate stand for peace.
That speech created a profound impression on all parties in the British House, and I venture to say in every quarter of the British islands. It met with immediate commendation from Labour and Liberal, and I cannot see how it can escape the commendation of every reasonable man. That is the tendency of the times. The big stick type of government is an outworn superstition, and whatever the motives of the Prime Minister may be- hon. gentlemen to our right who seek to prove that those motives are other than strictly virtuous are following a line of reasoning which I think is not strictly relevant to the question before the House. I believe the Prime Minister's action in itself is just what a modern democracy expects from a Prime Minister. To introduce a cut and dried proposition and try to ram it down the throat of parliament is the last thing that the ordinary citizen expects from a government to-day, and if that is the kind of government we are to get from the right hon. leader of the opposition, I think his chances of ever succeeding to power are exceedingly slim, because there is a temper abroad not only in Britain but in Canada which is absolutely against that spirit.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I contend that the debate so far, if it has proved anything at all, has proved that we cannot get any further intelligently without submitting this thing to a special committee. I have carefully followed the speeches and even the best of them, I think, are clouded over with a doubt. They have consisted for the most part of excerpts from different sources more or less well digested-less rather than more. One hon. gentleman said that we as a House could not foe expected to know much about marine affairs. I heartily agree with him after hearing some of the speeches to-night. I think as the debate has proceeded we have not had very much real light shed upon the problems of shipping. So I contend that the only thing we can do is to send this resolution to a special committee, where we can meet transportation experts face to face and get their opinions. We are not experts; I venture to say that most of us know as much about the horse marine as we know about the merchant marine.
I think probably three questions ought to be put to a special committee. We do not

need to ask if a combine exists; we are agreed that it does, and we are also agreed that some form of control is necessary. What we need ask the special committee is whether the combine which exists is hurtful or is one of the domestic type that is not ferocious to any degree. I do not know how the special committee would answer that question. It certainly has not been answered in this debate. There have been many attempts to do so, but I must confess that as yet I am no nearer deciding whether the combine is hurtful or not. Some hon. members have endeavoured to show that it is a monstrous affair, and others-mostly on my right-have attempted to show that it is comparatively harmless. Well, we do not know as yet, and we require the experts to get us anywhere in that direction. There is not enough knowledge among the whole of us to advance us one inch along that particular line. With respect to certain features of the situation I am more clear in my judgment than with respect to others. I believe that with regard to the important factor of grain the combine is not doing Canada very much harm. We have that proved in black and white. With respect to cattle we are in grave doubt. With respect to package and passenger freight we are equally in the dark. We cannot get any further- than we are to-night-and we are nowhere-unless we have the experts face to face with us, and we might as well recognize our helplessness. Another appropriate question to put before the committee is: What kind of control if necessary, will be best? Of course, if the combine is harmless no control will foe necessary. Does the proposal now before us promise to be effective in giving us control of ocean rates? I will not seek to enter into that question, because I believe we are just in the same position in regard to it as we are with respect to the nature of the combine itself. I do not think anyone to-night is qualified to give a. convincing opinion as to whether this proposition is going to work or not. There is just as much haziness in the House on that score as there is on other aspects of the case.
Now, certain alternatives have been put forward, and I think it is the duty of hon. members to put forward alternatives when they disagree with any proposal presented by the government. I have noticed no less than five or six alternatives submitted during the debate, some of them more or less practical, others purely idealistic. For instance, there is an alternative in the amendment. There are certain things we do not know about the motion; but there is nothing we do not know about the amendment; it is so perfectly

Ocean Shipping Rates
transparent. The amendment belongs entirely to the realm of improbabilities. The leader of the opposition in his excellent contribution to the debate argued that it was incompetent for Canada alone to set rates between here and Europe. Well, it was an impressive argument and delivered with some dramatic display, but I immediately thought to myself: Well, if that argument is good against Canada, how much more is it good against the empire setting rates for itself? Why, I think the leader of the official opposition has only to reflect for a moment to realize how absurd in a world like this it would be for the British Empire to try to set rates against other countries. The world would blow up at once. Farewell to the League of Nations, farewell to pacts of peace if once the British Empire set itself against the world in this respect. There is no such thing as inter-imperial trade pure and simple. The empire is just as much enmeshed in international trade as the other nations are, and it is beside the mark to say that Canada herself cannot control rates.
I have been very much interested in reading opinions expressed in the British newspapers on the Petersen contract. I notice in the Economist-a periodical quoted by the leader of the opposition-that the new president of the Chamber of Shipping, giving his opinion, said that Canada unfortunately-I suppose he meant certain people in Canada-believe that it was possible for her to do all of the selling and none of the buying. I believe there is a widespread conviction in Great Britain that Canada is out to sell Britain everything and buy nothing from her. If ever the empire is to be persuaded to control rates on behalf of the Dominion,, the empire would expect something from the dominions and that something is just what our friends to the right are unwilling to give them. They know that any bargain between us and Great Britain must be on a give and take basis, that if we are to get consideration in the matter of transportation we must give them consideration in this other regard. There is a certain amount of selfishness in an attitude of that kind, and I believe the time will never come when Great Britain, to whom shipping is so vital, will accept, a one-sided arrangement of that kind. I was somewhat interested in the view put forward by the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler). He deprecated the mixing of poetry and politics, but hon. members will notice that he was not so hesitant himself in entering the realm of prophecy, and it was very long range prophecy at that. He looked forward! to the time when the Canadian Pacific Railway 89
and the Canadian National Railways would join hands for the welfare of the country. He reminds me of the prophet who looked forward to the time when a little child would play with impunity on the hole of the asp and the lamb would lie down with the lion. I think it is a very attractive object but utterly idealistic, and wre do not always associate idealism with the mind of an hon. gentleman who is so practical in his method of reasoning.

Did the hon. member
for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) not imply that there was a possibility of the Canadian Pacific being taken over by the Canadian government?

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN-MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext:
I believe he did, but that possibility verges on the realm of impossibilities, a possibility which is far from being a probability.
I wish to enter the realm of prophecy on my own account, a little short-range prophecy for a change. There is one thing that has not been mentioned in this debate, and I am going to take upon myself the honour of mentioning it; and that is that in this country there are springing up mighty co-operative organizations. In the west we have monster grain co-operative pools. We have cattle pools also making great strides. Now these movements which are characteristic of the age spell co-operation, and I declare to-night, Mr. Speaker, that co-operation is the only alternative to combination, so we might as *well face it to-night. All these other things are doubtful, probably visionary, and will bring upon us the bitterness of disappointment, but in this movement which is so characteristic of our western life at the present time some of us see the only hope of checking the menace of these combinations. Those of us who have been interested in the co-operative movement for a good many years, as though it were a kind of religion, have wondered at times at the indifference of governments to the movement. It seems to me that the movement could not do better to-day than to throw its weight into the scale on behalf of a movement of that kind. I do not say that the co-operative movement in Canada is ripe for any practical proposal as to shipping and transportation, but it will be in that position very speedily. And I would suggest to the government that it keep its eyes upon that movement, because I believe that in a short time it will have arrived at a stage of development where some proposition of that kind will be very feasible, and it is the only thing in Canada that holds out

Ocean Shipping Rates

the least hope of successfully combating the combine. There is another short-range prophecy that I want to make, and the House will pardon me if I refer to the Hudson Bay railway.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN-MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext: Order, order.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN-MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext:
It hit somebody in a very tender place. It has seemed to me during this debate an odd thing that the Hudson Bay railway has never occurred to the minds of hon. members of this House as being an alternative proposal, perhaps not an alternative but a subsidiary proposal. I listened with great attention to the speech of the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Marler). His speeches in this House compel one to listen because they give signs that they originate in his own mind. They are not pale copies of dead philosophies, and so on. We may disagree with him considerably, but he speaks with such originality on Canadian problems that we are compelled to sit and listen to him, notwithstanding the extreme length of his speeches. When he was talking about the idea of universal subsidies in order to relieve the farmer in regard to his transportation problem, I wondered that his logical mind did not turn to the Hudson Bay railway, because if this government would complete the Hudson Bay railway-and there are only ninety short miles to build, and it is all graded-if they would spend a few million dollars, which would be a mere flea bite compared with this doubtful proposition before us to-night, in completing the Hudson Bay railway, they would bring the western farmer just one thousand miles nearer to Liverpool, and it is the worst thousand miles too, because while the ocean stretch is infested by sea serpents, this other thousand miles is infested by worse animals. At one stroke they would take that thousand miles of land transportation forever from the sphere in which it is at present, being now wide open to the exploiters of this country.
Talking about exploiters on the Atlantic ocean, they are not to be compared with the exploiters on the land. Somebody said something about not stopping at the shore. I would not begin at the shore. You want to go a long way this side of the shore if you are going to do the thing right. The fight on the ocean is problematic, but the fight on land is a real fight with those whom we know and we meet face to face with men of our own country. There is not much heroism in fighting the British merchant marine. It is of no political significance to rub them the wrong way. But it takes really hard fighting
IMr. Bird.]
to get rid of some of the pests that exist along our land transportation lines. By a very simple process, by spending just a few dollars which have been promised for many years by both political parties, they would cut out 1,000 miles. This would solve the grain problem. It would solve the cattle problem more than the grain problem. That is something which the western farmer can understand, but I question whether he can understand five words of the debate that has been going on during the last week. It means nothing to him; it is a medley of words, sound and fury signifying nothing to an inlander.
To return again to the attitude of my hon. friend to whom I refer, his attitude both in his speech on the Address and his speech this afternoon shows to me that a new light is breaking upon the statesmen of this country. I would say that my hon. friend ranks in that class. I think he has raised himself above the position of mere politician. I think he has endeavoured to look at the problems of this country in a fair, broad, statesmanlike way, perhaps not from the particular angle that we view them and not arriving at the conclusions that we arrive at. You could not entrust subsidies in the hands of politicians with whom we have been blessed for the past number of years; but I believe that the process is coming about by which this parliament, when it is thoroughly representative of the people and when the-people have proper control over it, will be-able to subsidize necessitous concerns of this country. I look forward to that age. I believe a complex civilization cannot go on without some form of mutual help; but this all assumes a very much advanced form of parliamentary government, and I am afraid that as yet we have not reached that stage. We admit the principle immediately when we consider transportation rates on land. carried. So that any words of mine will be futile. But I feel it my duty to place some of my views with respect to this important question before the House. We were assured from the outset that our good friends to the left would not see the party directly opposite in difficulty; their life boat is always to be seen coming through the mist when the government is in trouble, as my leader (Mr. Meighen) observed. However, the government is not in trouble in this instance. The Prime Minister doubtless expected when this proposition was put before the country that the agricultural population would be swept off their feet in favour of it, but for once some of the agriculturists have displayed a little incredulity and it is necessary to prolong debate in order to bring them to terms. We see them hour by hour being brought around to the government's way of thinking. With respect to the government's attitude in this matter, I can see that the Prime Minister did not feel quite happy when he perceived that it was not going over as strongly as he wished it to do. He is looking for a place on which to land; he is tired of the sea and I am sure that terra firma will loom up when this matter reaches the committee stage. I do not believe that the Petersen proposal will be ratified by this parliament; I do not believe that the public of Canada are in favour of it. It is folly to expect that ten small ships will have any influence on the immense shipping of the seven seas.
I come now to the immigration phase of this subject, on which the minister in charge of the measure (Mr. Low) dwelt with some emphasis. He stressed the great benefits that would accrue to the immigration problem in the operation of these ships. The Prime Minister touched upon it more lightly than the Minister of Trade and Commerce. The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Macdonald), if I remember rightly, did not touch on it at all. The reason was that a few well expressed remarks on the part of the hon. member for Burrard (Mr. Clark) entirely dissipated any hopes in that direction. No accommodation is to be provided on these ships for immigrants. We know that in Europe thousands are waiting to get into the United States when they can under the quota laws, willing to pay the rates exacted by the steamships. These people do not want to come here. This is not the time to discuss the reason why, and I assure you the Petersen line will not bring immigrants here who would not come otherwise. So that you can consider the immigration argument pretty well dissipated.
Another argument is based on the alleged exorbitant freight rates on the ocean. But there is not one jot or tittle of evidence to show that freight rates are exorbitant on the Atlantic.. We have not one tittle of evidence that the steamships in the combine-and doubtless it is a combine; I do not see how it could very well be otherwise and give good service-are paying huge dividends or even making adequate profits. On the other hand we have the fact that our merchant marine, although it has .been sitting in at the conference, has been losing money. That is a very good argument that the combine as a whole is not making exorbitant profits; at least, we have no reason to assume that they are, so that is a very doubtful argument. We know that high rates are being charged on the ocean, but we know also that in these progressive days the ship-owners have to improve their services from time to time. We know that they have gone through very difficult times. We know that the Cunard line at one time was almost down and out, requiring assistance. These lines must vie with each other in giving service that is adequate to meet the demands of a rather critical travelling public, yet they must make money, they must make profits in order to maintain the service, keep the ships in proper condition and make renewals from time to time. Unless it can be proved that they are making excessive and exorbitant profits, that argument falls to the pound. And these two arguments, the one with respect to immigration and the other with respect to exorbitant freight charges, were the two strongest arguments used in favour of this resolution.

speechtext: Th ; House was pretty nearly ready for the question, Mr. Speaker, an hour ago. We are faced at this time with perhaps one of the most unfair actions on the part of the government, one of the most flagram, departures from the long recognized practice of this House, and that is: bringing to a vote, in this House, without notice, on a Friday night a major measure. I am quite aware, Mr. Speaker, and you with your long experience in parliament are no doubt equally well aware, that there is no rule of the House calling for this special consideration to be given to members; but there has been a practice stretching back as long as the memory of the oldest member of this House, and much longer, that no major question shall be brought to a vote on Friday night. And why? Not that it ever advantages me a particle; I happen to come, Mr. Speaker, from the extreme west, and am fated with some other members to attend here at all times. I have not the privilege of going to my home every week end, as have members from Ontario and Quebec. But there is perhaps a third or more of the members of this House who so arrange their affairs that they go home on Friday afternoon or Friday evening regularly. It is well known and understood what has been the practice. It is this: That on Fridays, government measures that are not of major importance shall be before the House, usually such matters as estimates and the like, or measures that are not looked upon as controversial. I venture this assertion, Sir, and I invite you to search your memory for the past twenty-five or thirty years that you have graced a position in this House, and see if you can recall-I certainly cannot- a single case where without notice, without previous arrangement, a major question has been brought to a vote on a Friday. There was absolutely no thought of this matter being brought to a vote to-night, and when our whip consulted with the government authorities after the session opened to-day he was coolly informed that a vote would be taken to-night.
