speechtext:
The proper parliamentary procedure is this. Primarily this is a government resolution dealing with money matters, and it is the peculiar prerogative of the government to deal with such matters. It is the primary practice of constitutional government that the administration submit any measure to parliament as its considered judgment, and by that considered judgment it stands or falls. That is responsible government. That is where we differ with some hon. members in this House, not because we are old-fashioned, not because we do not appreciate progress, but because we are convinced that responsible government is the best system under which a country can progress. I am quite aware that another practice might be adopted, that parliament should ipse dixit, be like a county council, and that measures might be introduced from any quarter, here, there or elsewhere, and no one take responsibility for them. But I ask hon. gentlemen to ponder what sort of chaotic condition would this country be in within a measurably short period of years if that course were followed? Again I repeat that the practice we are standing for, the practice we are insisting shall be followed in this parliament, is the practice that has been proven for hundreds of years to be the best. What is that practice? What are the rules of this House? In heaven's name, Mr. Speaker, let us amend the rules and do things in an orderly way if we are going to depart from the regular practice. What is the practice in dealing with this resolution and this amendment? If the government desire to send this contract to a committee later on, let them introduce a resolution accordingly. But why inject it into this debate? I would ask hon. gentlemen to use just simple common sense in the matter. Here is a signed and sealed contract. No one disputes that the contract cannot be changed or varied except with the consent of the two parties to it. Here is a resolution. It is before this House to put its stamp of approval upon it. Let me read it:
That to give the government of Canada control over certain ocean rates, it is expedient-
What?
-it is expedient to ratify and confirm the agreement between His Majesty and Sir William Petersen.
That is what we are considering in plain simple English. If this parliament says, "Yes, we ratify that agreement," I ask hon. gentlemen, Mr. Speaker, what position will we find ourselves in if two, three or four weeks from now we come back and say, "Why, we did not know what we were doing, we acted hastily without information; now we want tc change this whole thing".

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN-MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext:
If you will allow me
to finish my answer-yes, absolutely we are ratifying this. But this is where British parliamentary practice and Canadian parliamentary practice are sound. What does it do? It provides for certain processes to be followed. What are they for? To safeguard the rights of the people or those who desire to criticize or object. What is the process in this case? The first thing is the introduction of the notice of motion. Then we come to the position we are in now, that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the House to go into committee. The next thing is that the committee considers the resolution. The resolution is reported out of committee, then it is read a second time. Then there is a bill based upon that. Then leave is asked to introduce the bill. Then next it is read the first time. After that it is read the second time. That is what some hon. gentlemen call red tape, unnecessary parliamentary methods, something that should be largely done away with, and they say "let us take a short cut." The point is this: such processes are fixed in our rules and regulations for the purpose of protecting the public in just such cases as this. Ordinary bills, which on the face of them are non-controversial, we pass through these stages very rapidly, and the procedure is called useless red tape, but it is nothing of the kind. These formalities are prescribed in our rules for the purpose of protecting just such important measures as this. What I want to point out to the House is this: we might very well use the analogy of the budget. There is a process followed in that case, and it is virtually the same process as this. This resolution has the same effect as the budget. This is a vote of money. We are voting here at least fifteen million.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN-MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext: At what stage in the procedure is the resolution ratified, or is not the whole procedure necessary before ratification?

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN-MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext:
Absolutely. The hon.
gentleman is quite right. It has to go through

the procedure I have mentioned, and finally come to a third reading. There are certain stages in the procedure of this House that through long parliamentary practice are recognized as very important stages. This is what I want to place before my hon. friends to my left, because I apprehend what is in their mind3: they say they are not quite satisfied that this is a good measure. Some distinctly disagree with it. Some of them, and practically all, say they do not like the general idea, the trend of the legislation, but they say, "We are convinced that something should be done." We agree with them. I do not think anybody in the House disagrees with that statement, but what I want to put before my hon. friends is this: they rest their case for a complete departure from parliamentary rules of procedure on what? Upon the word of the Prime Minister interjected in the middle of a debate. I am not impugning the Prime Minister's word, nor am I challenging his sincerity. Let us take it at a hundred per cent for the sake of argument, but if the Prime Minister is absolutely sincere in this, before bringing this measure in a finished form before parliament for ratification, why did he not move for the appointment of a special committee? What is the resolution my right hon. friend will have to move? It will be a resolution something to this effect: that a special committee consisting of fifteen members, or whatever number he chooses to name, shall be appointed for the purpose of doing certain things. The order of reference will be the whole value of that committee. My hon. friends do not know what the order of reference is to be. They are voting blindly on this on the assumption that the order of reference is going to be of a character that will please and satisfy them. Suppose the Prime Minister says in his order of reference that he moves for a committee of fifteen members to be appointed for the purpose of considering this agreement and for the purpose of reporting to the House its finding. What better are you off in that case than you would be if you adopted such course right here?
The Prime Minister states that so far as this agreement is concerned he stands or falls by it. Let us take another supposition: suppose my right hon. friend goes the full limit of the expectation of my hon. friends to my left and moves a committee be appointed for the purpose of inquiring into the alleged effect of the combination on the north Atlantic in restraint of trade, and to ascertain if general rates are too high, and to .report, and if there can be some measure of control, to secure it, and

Ocean Shipping Rates
report their findings to the House. Assume he goes that distance-and that or something similar to that is what they want-what was there to hinder him from moving that at any time in the last three weeks or a month? For the first few weeks after the opening of the House no committee sat at all. A committee might have been holding sittings dhring that period. In the Speech from the Throne he forecast this measure, and stated that the government had made up its mind on this question. He stated it had made up its mind on the 24th December, or before Mr. Preston put- in his report. He, Mr. Preston, says in his letter contained in his report that the government's mind was made up as to what it would do, and is precisely what this resolution says: to organize a company for the purpose of competing with the North Atlantic Steamship Conference. This is not a new thing. The government knew about it when parliament met. If the Prime Minister is sincere, and if he was sincere, why did he not introduce such resolution andl have this committee hold sittings before we are asked to ratify the agreement at all?
I ask my hon. friends, are we to take what the rules of the House declare is the interpretation of this proceeding; or are we to vote in a manner which virtually ratifies the agreement and then trust to the Prime Minister to bring in a resolution later on with the proper order of reference? I will give my hon. friends another procedure which could have been followed. When notice of the resolution was given and it was placed on the order paper, it was still open to the Prime Minister to appoint a committee, and it has been open to the Prime Minister ever since the debate started, to let the debate stand in abeyance, appoint a committee, and have the committee report before we were called upon to vote upon the resolution. I ask my hon. friends as sensible men, how do we vote on this? We vote in the light of the information we have. That i3 how I am called upon to vote. I am not called upon to take the evidence of the hon. member opposite and his interpretation of some circuitous process to get some further evidence that we know nothing about. I am not called upon to do that, and he has not the right to ask members of parliament on this side, or any other side of the House, to accept his word in this matter, and I should not be expected to conform to that procedure. I accept the plain English of this resolution.
I want to examine the resolution for a moment. I am not going into the agreement, or going to again go through the process, but I want to examine the procedure.
We have two things before us and one of them is that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair. I have under my hand an interpolation of the Prime Minister to the speech that was delivered a few minutes ago by the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Shaw). That hon. member had just stated that he accepted the word of the Prime Minister that this resolution would go to a committee ultimately and ample scope would be given to consider it and vary it in any way they chose. He said he accepted that. But the Prime Minister rose and interpolated this:
Not only will we do that, but as soon as this resolution under consideration carries I intend to move, and before it goes into committee at all-
And I want hon. members to follow me-
-before it goes into committee of the whole House,
I am prepared to move the appointment of this special committee.
Let us examine his position. Surely the rules of the House and plain, simple English ought to govern. The resolution is that Mr. Speaker leave the chair. If the resolution is carried, ordinarily what position are we in? The position we are in is this, that Mr. Speaker is out of the chair and this House is in committee of the Whole on this resolution. It is not competent for the Prime Minister to interject such a resolution as the one he mentions now.

speechtext:
Hitherto the position was
that what would be done would be this, that the bill on its second reading would be referred to a special committee. That has been told us time and time again. What I am arguing and pleading for in this House is simply to let us stand by the rules of the House and the plain English of this measure. Let me illustrate my point. Eminent authorities on law have pointed out certain things in this agreement. What have we had in reply? We have had in reply this from the Prime Minister: I do not care what is in the agreement: I say so and so. Surely we are not going to
Ocean Shipping Rates

be called upon to accept a position of that kind. We are not children; we are not here to accept the ipse dixit of the Prime Minister; we are here to deal with measures in black and white and plain English. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb), and several other ministers of the crown, who have had long experience in parliamentary life, know that one of the most important things in legislation is to have measures carefully, properly and clearly drafted, and there is no sense or use in introducing to parliament a measure that does not convey the intention of the government, if it is a government measure. If the Prime Minister has any desire to change this, if, as he says, his private interpretation of this measure is what will control, then why does he not and why has he not embodied it in the resolution itself? Further than that, when this resolution passes this committee, it is not competent for private members to change the principle of the bill that is based upon the resolution. I know it is quite competent for parliament to reverse its own action. But for instance, this resolution, when it carries, authorizes the payment to Sir William Petersen of a certain sum of money as a subsidy, not as a charter, as the Minister of National: Defence (Mr, Macdonald) would have us believe. It is not a charter or any distant relation of a charter; it is a subsidy pure and simple, and no private member of this House has any right to substitute anything else for it. There is one of two courses, one of two destinies for this bill and only those, in the minds of the government now, in the mind of the Prime Minister as he sits in this House-I am not quite sure which of the two he intends to take-one is a deliberate intention to kill this measure in committee and then to go to the country at large and say: We tried to do our 'best, but we were defeated in parliamentary committee on the matter. The other is to use his majority in the committee, which he will have over both oppositions, to force this thing through, then to come back to the House and say it was carried after careful investigation, and go before the country and say; This was given careful consideration by a parliamentary committee, approved by that committee, approved by a majority of the House and, therefore, we are justified in carrying it into effect. One of these two courses the Prime Minister has determined to pursue. It is all balderdash to my mind-the idea of giving to a committee an opportunity to study carefully this matter. Let hon. gentlemen take

note of the voluminous reports on this subject. Do hon. gentlemen who have read those reports expect to get in that committee any better information than they can get from the reports of the Shipping Committee of 1909, or 'the Dominions Royal Commission, or the committee that sat in 1918 on shipbuilding, or the latest one, the Imperial Shipping Committee? Any one of those will give us not only British but Canadian testimony. 7. here is any quantity of it and it has been conned over by hon. gentlemen in this House. There is nothing you can bring up in a committee that will help to solve the question any more than that.

speechtext: Am I to understand that my hon. friend contends that this government could spend any money simply because a resolution had been voted without a bill following the resolution in the regular course?

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN-MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext: No, I have already outlined the procedure. My hon. friend probably did not hear me.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN-MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext: I followed my hon. friend.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN-MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext:
I carefully followed the
proper parliamentary procedure. I will do it again so that there will be no mistake in regard to my position. I said, first, there was notice given of a resolution; second, the resolution was moved into committee of the Whole; third, the resolution was reported; fourth, it was read a second time and agreed to; fifth, leave to introduce a bill was asked for; sixth, the bill was read a first time; seventh, the bill was read a second time; eighth, it was sent to a committee, and lastly, it came back to the House and was read a third time. That is the procedure.
Let me refer to the amendment. You cannot brush aside this resolution by any simple gesture, saying: Let us slip it out of the way and we shall have it up in the committee in some fashion or another. There is the resolu- ' tion for our consideration. It is one of the most important documents that has been introduced in this House during this session. It involves the expenditure of a large sum of money. It makes possible the expenditure of an unlimited sum, as I want hon. gentlemen to realize as well. In addition to that, it deals with a very serious principle, that of subsidizing ocean steamships in competition . with others in connection with the freight handling business. We do not agree with that. We have been charged that we have offered no constructive criticism. This is what we suggest, and I invite bon. gentlemen to give some thought to this. We say that

Ocean Shipping Rates
we do not agree with this Petersen contract at all. We want to reject it absolutely and we say that, instead of Mr. Speaker leaving the chair and the House going into committee on this question, this be done:
That Mr. Speaker do not now leave the chair but that it be resolved: That effective control of ocean rates can be exercised only with the co-operation of all portions of the empire, and by a body on which all are represented, and the contract made by the government with Sir William Petersen, based on the report of W. T, R. Preston, is ill-advised, costly and futile and unworthy of the serious consideration of this House.
This is what we offer to the House. There is not in this amendment a word that is inconsistent with the report, the advice and the recommendation of the Agriculture committee of 1923, upon which the Prime Minister now says he bases his measure. I am not going to read the report again as it has been read several times. What did it recommend? First, it cited and reviewed a great deal of the testimony and said that it was a tremendously important question; that it was a question that required the utmost care and consideration. It suggested a reference to the International Institute of Agriculture at Rome. Then it recommended that we should cooperate with other parts of the empire in bringing about some stabilization and control of freight rates. We suggest that there should be co-operation with all portions of the empire.
My right hon. leader yesterday showed with such clarity that all must have seen the point and accepted it as beyond contravention, that the government couid not possibly control rates between Canada and any other country. We could not control rates between Canada and the United States nor between Canada and Great Britain. We could control them by owning the ships and carrying freight at a loss, but we could exercise no control nor could we direct the transportation of freight between this country and another. And that is what the amendment says;.it declares that in order to secure that control there must be co-operation with other parts of the empire. My right hon. friend, the Prime Minister, in his speech, in a somewhat light vein I admit, said that the time may come when an international board may be set up. Well, I know of no better way of starting than by setting up an inter-imperial board which would comprehend half of the liner steamship tonnage of the world, thus taking a long step towards the goal which the Prime Minister has in view at some distant date in the future. We say that there should be co-operation, in which all parts of the empire should be
represented; and further we say that this contract entered' into by the government with Sir William Petersen is ill-advised, costly and futile. I invite hon. gentlemen to examine these last few words. I have not heard any hon. gentlemen in this House, with the exception possibly of the minister himself (Mr. Low) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), say anything else than that the agreement was ill-advised and that they questioned the wisdom of proceeding with it. I have not heard one single gentleman say anything to the contrary, nor have I read in any leading journal in this country, with the exception of the Manitoba Free Press, any editorial which openly commended the contract. Take my hon. friend from St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Mailer); he knows perfectly well that the contract is undoubtedly ill-advised and he knows it is costly and futile. Nor would he und'er any circumstances stand in this House and say he approved of it. Yet the hon. gentleman will vote for it; he will vote in support of it. The hon. member knows perfectly well that the whole thing is absolutely futile; he knows that it is in direct contravention of the veiy policy about which he has been speaking so learnedly in the last few months. There is not a single thing in this contract, not a principle of it, not one of its terms, which is consonant with his attitude during recent months. Yet he will vote for it.

kind would ensue. Certainly; let the Prime
Minister adjourn the debate and suspend this thing. If the Prime Minister is sincere that is what he will do. My hon. friend has put his finger on the spot. What object is there in forcing the matter to a vote and placing us in the compromising position of supporting or rejecting it-supporting it when hon. gentlemen desire to reject it? What is the object in doing that? I venture the suggestion right now that if the experts on our rules were to look carefully into this matter it is doubtful whether the Prime Minister's motion would be considered in order at all. It would be but sound parliamentary procedure for the Prime Minister to move the adjournment of the debate, or have one of his supporters move it, and then appoint a committee. That is sound parliamentary procedure and certainly it is the plain common sense of the situation, if he wants to play the game square with hon. gentlemen to my left whom he wants to support the measure. I am not suggesting to hon. gentlemen to my left that they should line up with us and vote against the government to put them out of office. Not at all; I should prefer the government to stay in office a little while longer, for they are killing themselves faster than we could kill them. I do not want to defeat the government now. But if half a dozen honourable gentlemen would politely tell the Prime Minister that the ordinary parliamentary procedure should be followed, if they would challenge his sincerity by asking him to have the debate adjourned and to appoint a committee to investigate the matter, they could secure the object they have in view. But my hon. friends are not particularly anxious

to investigate the Petersen contract; what they want to do is to investigate the broad question of ocean freight rates.

I had not the slightest thought of occupying the House at this time of night in connection with this debate, but I feel I cannot allow the remarks of my hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) to pass without making some observations.
It has been my pleasure and my privilege to act as whip of this party now for nearly four years. I am glad to say we have managed to get on without any misunderstanding, with an exchange of courtesy and fair play in our proceedings during all that time, and I would like to pay the whip of the government party the compliment of saying that I am of the opinion that if he had not been laid up at his house with sickness, we would not have had the situation we have to-night. I asked the minister if he would say when the government determined to force a vote. He said he did not know the government did determine to force a vote.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN-MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN-MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext:
That is a different thing. I concede at once the right of the government to force a vote whenever they want to. But I do think that the custom of years and the courtesy of years should play some part in that determination. I want to say that when I discussed this morning in no exceptional way, but in the ordinary way, the matter of those who had yet to speak, not to obstruct, but to make speeches, there was no suggestion on the part of the government whips that there would be a vote to-day. Not until I got into the House at three o'clock was there ever such a suggestion, and I feel it my duty in order that those at all events in my own group may see that the trouble we have got to-day is one that cannot be laid at my door, to make the situation clear. I think I have always tried to be fair in conducting the business of this Houise so far as this party is concerned, and I believe the whips with whom I have worked will do me the justice of saying so. But it has certainly been forced upon me that we have now reached the stage where one of two things must happen:	We must
either continue to be frank and fair with each other, and maintain the customs of the past, or else come to the conclusion that they are to be lat an end.
Now I got this note after three o'clock. This was after a preliminary talk when there was no suggestion that there was to be a vote 90
to-day. It has been known for two weeks that we had eight or ten more speakers, and I suggest it would be hardly fair to ask them to speak at two or three o'clock in the morning. As a matter of fact, most of the government members from Quebec want to go home at 3.30 on Friday afternoon, and frankly I may say that most of our members from Ontario want to go away at eleven o'clock on Friday night. I naturally wished to avoid this vote to-night, and I suggested that it could go over till Tuesday, that the budget could be introduced on Tuesday, and then could be left over a day or two for consideration, and that we could then go on with this, and I promised that so far 'as we were concerned there would be a vote on -this resolution on Tuesday night.
I got this letter from one of the government assistant whips. He did not say to me: There will be a vote to-night. He said, "We will try to vote to-day." I thought that was a little strange, and I wrote back and said, "Does this mean you intend to force a vote? If it does, I do not think it is fair, for I have had no notice, and I have not notified my members. Nobody expected a vote." The answer came back, and I give him credit for being frank with me, "Yes that is the intention." I have not the slightest doubt the government made up their minds yesterday to force a vote on this resolution to-night. I notice in the House to-night members who have not been here for quite a long time, who have come from a long distance, upon word from somebody upon the government side to be here on hand to vote.
I want to say most emphatically that if we are to be fair and frank with each other the least courtesy that could have been shown to me was to tell me this morning, at all events, when I was negotiating for the proceedings of to-day, that there was to be a vote to-night, so that I could notify the members. But that was kept back. Now I appeal to the Prime Minister. I do not think that I suffer from a chronic grouch, but I admit that I am disappointed. To me this is one of the most unfortunate days since I have been in the House of Commons. I do not think it a creditable performance. I do not know who is absolutely responsible for it, but I do not believe the whips are. I think if we are going to use the whips at all in the House, then surely we must be fair with each other. If I had been asked to agree to a day and had refused, or had been unreasonable, it would have been quite in order to say: We will force a vote. But I have never been asked to do it. I see the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) in

Ocean Shipping Rates

his place. He once occupied the position I occupy, the whip of the opposition, and I wonder what he would have thought if he had been treated that way.
I have said enough, I think, to show that this proceeding is not fair. It comes to this: If we cannot be fair with each other, the only way to get business done will be to do business at arm's length, and to cancel all pairs. That is not my desire. I would be very sorry to see that done. I appeal to the Prime Minister: I do not think we have been treated fairly on this occasion, and I trust that if we do come to some understanding for the future, that a repetition of this incident will not take place. If it does, then so far as I am concerned I would no longer want to be whip of the Conservative party, for I would be unable to do business with the whip on the other side under those conditions.

Again this week I mentioned that the budget would be brought down this week. I made it perfectly plain that if we did not get it down this week, we would bring it down on Tuesday next, and at the very outset I intimated that when the budget was brought down it would take precedence over everything else, and that we hoped to conclude the budget debate by Easter.
Now this resolution has been before the House eight or ten days. It has been understood all along that we wished to get the bill to a committee before the budget debate came on. My hon. friend knows that Monday is private members' day, and that if we did not take the course of getting this vote to-night the chance of getting this bill to a committee might remain over until after the recess. I do not think anyone would wish that. To-day I was told that no undertaking could be given by my hon. friend that this bill would get to a committee even on Thursday, if Thursday were set apart for further debate. When that intimation was given to me I made it perfectly clear that we would have to take the vote to-night.

speechtext:
My point is that under
the rules this resolution must pass through committee of the Whole. The motion now is that it do not; and for the simple reason that the motion is contrary to the rules it cannot be in order.

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN-MOTION FOR RATIFICATION DISCUSSED
speechtext:
Will my hon. friend see
this? I know he will see it if he thinks of it: You cannot have a resolution before two committees at the same time. It is now resolved to send the resolution to a special committee, and that committee will submit its report.

Motion agreed to.
On motion of Mr. Mackenzie King the House adjourned at 1.20 am. (Saturday).
Monday, March 23, 1925
